subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because of the various representations which have been made to me by some hon. members of this house, and by various persons, agencies and organizations in western Canada, with the permission of the house I desire to make a statement concerning the strike of some 350 west coast grain elevator employees which has halted the movement of grain to export markets and from the farm to country elevators. If I may have permission I should like to make this statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext: Does the hon. member have leave to make this statement?

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext:
The collective agreement between the grain workers' union and the five operators of the elevators expired on December 1, 1959, and negotiations were entered into by the parties for a new agreement. The parties were unable themselves to settle the terms of a new collective agreement, and I appointed a west coast conciliation officer to assist them. When my officer was unsuccessful I appointed a conciliation board in March, and the board made its recommenda-tions'for the settlement of the dispute in June. The chairman of the board and the employers' nominee made a majority report containing recommendations, and the trade union nominee made a minority report.
The companies agreed to accept the majority recommendations, 'but the union delayed in stating its position and it was not until October 31 that the representative of the union advised that its members had rejected

Statement on Grain Handlers Strike unanimously the recommendations of the conciliation board and that it was making application to its international headquarters for permission to take a strike vote.
My department was advised on November 7 that the union had served a strike notice on the grain companies effective midnight Tuesday, November 8, and the strike took place at the time scheduled. On November 9 I communicated by telephone with both parties concerned, urging them to meet again with my conciliation officer in an endeavour to settle their' differences. They agreed to do so, and meetings were then continued.
Late on Friday, November 11, because of the unsuccessful attempt by my own conciliation officer to bring about an agreement, I appointed Mr. F. Craig Munroe, Q.C., of New Westminster, British Columbia, an industrial inquiry commissioner to mediate the dispute, and the commissioner commenced his meetings with the parties on Monday, November 14. He has met the parties constantly since that time and is still discussing the settlement of the dispute with them.
Mr. Speaker, it will be seen from what I have said that everything possible has been done under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to assist the ' parties in reaching a settlement. They have had the assistance of a conciliation officer, conciliation board, post-conciliation board mediation, and now they are receiving the advice and assistance of an industrial inquiry commissioner. I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that all possible aid has been given to the parties, and the officers of my department have been in touch with them at all stages of'the dispute.
The employees and employers have complied with all the procedures contained in our legislation, and the strike is not in violation of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. There are no provisions under the act nor in any other legislation which give the government of Canada authority to have prevented the strike from taking place or to compel resumption of work. We have no authority to go beyond what we have done to prevent a stoppage of work. Settlement of this dispute clearly depends upon the parties themselves. We have provided them with all levels of mediation, but they themselves must recognize the damage that is being done to our western economy in the loss of sales involved in the export of grain, and they must be prepared to make the mutual concessions necessary for a fair and reasonable settlement. I am very hopeful that having regard to the public interest they will be prepared to accept such

proposals as may be worked out by the commissioner for the settlement of the dispute and the resumption of operations.
In my telegram appointing the commissioner I said to the parties:
It is of vital importance to the entire Canadian economy that the movement of grain for export and from farms to local elevators be resumed at the earliest possible moment and to this end I have appointed Mr. F. Craig Munroe, Q.C., New Westminster, British Columbia an industrial inquiry commissioner to make inquiry into the dispute affecting the Vancouver terminal grain elevators and to assist the parties to the dispute in reaching agreement on all issues that stand in the way of resumption of work. In the discussions that have been carried on in the period since the date of the strike notice both parties have been fixed and rigid in their attitudes toward the issues in dispute and now must direct their whole attention to the making of mutual concessions to effect a settlement in the public interest. I request the earnest co-operation of the parties with the commissioner in reaching a fair and reasonable settlement. The commissioner will be assisted by Mr. G. R. Currie, departmental chief industrial relations officer, Vancouver.
Many persons and farm organizations have made representations to me concerning this dispute, and I have advised them of our constant efforts to assist the parties in reaching a settlement and have urged them to bring their pressure directly to bear on the trade union and employers involved in the dispute.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext:
This unhappy strike, affecting as it does the business of grain marketing, is a matter of great national importance as well as being of immediate significance to every western grain producer. It is, therefore, of the first importance to bring it to an end at the earliest possible date, and all members of this house must hope that the efforts which are being made to this end will be successful.
The legal position may be that which has been described by the minister, and we all recognize the hon. gentleman's difficulties; but we must hope that he will maintain his concern and make every effort which he and the government can legally make to intervene in order to bring this strike to an end. We all wish him well in that endeavour.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext:
I am pleased that the minister took this opportunity to inform the house of some of the actions which have been taken by himself and his department. This is a situation which affects not only the grain handling companies and the employees; it has very widespread repercussions among many Canadians, particularly among tens of thousands of grain producers on the prairies. It interferes with the normal transport of grain and, if it has not already done so, it could lead, if prolonged, to a loss of sales in addition to the present

delay in the marketing of grain. I have said on a previous occasion, and I urge again now, that the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Agriculture and, I would suggest also, the Minister of Veterans Affairs should proceed immediately to Vancouver to interview the various parties to the dispute in the hope that a settlement might be reached at an early date.
The government has taken this very kind of action in an endeavour to avoid a railway strike. Although the date is now late, I suggest that similar action should be taken by the government at this time. I urge the Prime Minister and the cabinet to have these three cabinet ministers proceed to Vancouver to discuss with both parties the issues involved, in the hope that a settlement may be arrived at immediately.

Mr. Speaker, in my answer I related the fact that 14.2 million bushels have already been exported from Canada, and we will require all the Durum wheat that we are able to get from the farmers to meet the commitments.

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses FINANCE

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, November 21, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) -Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee of loans made by banks to proprietors of small business enterprises, for the improvement and modernization of premises and equipment, and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the said measure shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have heard from the opposition speakers how they support this resolution. We have also heard from them as to the defects that they think may be inherent in the resolution.
According to the last census there are some
400,000	small businesses in Canada. Those figures were based on a turnover of $300,000 a year. With the growth of the country I think we can say that we still have 400,000 small businesses falling within the limits of the legislation; that is, of $250,000 a year annual turnover. Some 90 per cent of these small businesses are in the retail and service field, and of that 90 per cent, again 90 per cent of that number will fall into the range of annual turnover to be covered by this bill.
With regard to manufacturing, there are some 35,000 to 40,000 manufacturing companies in Canada. It is estimated that three quarters of these will fall within the terms of the new bill. The bill, as we have been told by the minister, will allow a maximum loan of up to $25,000 on a medium term basis with repayment over ten years, and will provide credit facilities which small business has not had available up to this time.
Formerly, small business could have working capital from a bank, which was on a demand basis and was not for the purpose of acquiring additional equipment or extending premises, and was not on a medium or long term basis. Opposition speakers have tried to point out that the government has had no concern for small business, whereas the record shows that this has been the first government to actually bring in legislation expressly designed to aid and benefit small business. It started, naturally enough, with the setting up of a staff of civil servants in the small business division of the Department of Trade and Commerce to study the needs and requirements of small business and advise the government and be a vehicle to convey small business needs and requirements to the government.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made quite a point of the fact that there was

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses no attempt, as far as he could find out from the blue book last year, to carry on the functions of this division, whereas if he would look at the telephone book he would find that the small business division is intact and has been working continuously since it was set up.
The point was made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that this government was copying from his party's platform, and he seemed to regret that the facilities of the industrial development bank had not been used in this legislation. The industrial development bank has some 12 branches spread across Canada, whereas the chartered banks have some 3,000 branches. Small business is not necessarily found entirely in big cities. Small business, as the name implies, is spread throughout the country; in villages and towns as well as in major cities. It is only through the medium of the chartered banks, with their widespread coverage of the entire country, that small business can be adequately serviced, because small business will always have branches near them where they can go to secure these loans.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam stated that his group was in agreement with the principle behind this resolution, but at one point in his speech he said he regretted the insufficiency of the resolution and at another he referred to the inadequacy of the resolution. In fact the resolution is neither insufficient nor inadequate. The minister has pointed out that it covers almost the entire scope of Canadian business activity, a field which has not been covered before by government legislation or government help. At the present time, through its agencies, the government provides assistance to housing, fishing and farming. Now, through the present measure, the government will be aiding in the fields of manufacturing, wholesale operations, retail business, service industries, tourist establishments, co-operatives and the like. It would be interesting to hear of an area of Canadian small business or Canadian business in general which is not covered here.
The view that the industrial development bank should handle these loans is certainly not valid. In fact it would almost appear now as though the industrial development bank, because of the wide range of this resolution, should vacate the field of small loans up to $25,000, because I feel that the resolution before us will take care of practically all loans of this magnitude.
Further criticism of the resolution-and I say this with the most kindly feelings toward the hon. member concerned-has been that perhaps it is not good because we are being unkind rather than kind when we offer to
IMr. Broome.]
lend money. This was the view of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. Certainly the government cannot guarantee that a man who secures a loan under the terms of this resolution will be able to repay it. The government cannot foresee what his problems may be. The government can, however, make funds available to some 400,000 small businesses in Canada through the medium of the established banking system, and it will be up to the bank managers to assess whether a loan is a good one to make. By reason of the government guarantee a bank manager will be able to guide himself by the record of the person concerned and be in a position to make the loan without the necessity of security which under regular banking procedure would have to be provided.
Here we are dealing with some 400,000 employers of labour, whether they employ carpenters or electricians for the renovation of their premises, or workers in manufacturing plants making tow trucks for gasoline stations, or a refrigerated showcase for a grocery store. The effect of this measure will be felt in every corner of Canada. It would hardly be possible to overestimate the importance of this resolution, not only as it will provide work and much needed improvements to premises but also as it will bring help to a substantial section of our business community, a section which has been ignored year after year by previous governments.
This measure will have 100 per cent support in this house. It will have the support of the C.C.F. party and the Liberal party. I have been trying to point out, at least in part of this speech, how diligently spokesmen for those parties have tried to find some weakness in the resolution which they might criticize. They have not as yet been able to find anything, though we have been told that when the bill is available they may be more successful.
I rather doubt that, because the resolution is simple. It is a plan which can be easily carried out, since we have the means to carry it out, as I said earlier, through our present banking system. The cut-off point is the $250,000 annual turnover. There must be a cut-off point; there must be a separation of small business from big business, and wherever that point is placed there will be some enterprises which fall just below the line and some which fall just above it. That is the way it is with all government measures. Such measures must define the areas which they are to cover, and I think the government has, if anything, stretched a point by deciding on a figure of $250,000. The amount of money which can be made available is $25,000, and the term for repayment is 10 years. All this makes good common sense.

I think, as I said before, that this will be one of the most important measures and most effective measures to be presented to the house this session.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
First of all I want to say how pleased I am that the government has decided to come forward with a measure which will provide at least intermediate term credit to small businesses. For a number of years I have taken a personal interest in this subject, as the record of the banking and commerce committee will show. As long ago as 1956 I advocated action to provide loan facilities for small business. I think that making this provision through the banks is necessary and desirable, though I shall have some further remarks to make on this general subject in a few minutes.
I feel that the government might have broadened this particular aspect. Although this seems to be part of the government's package to deal with unemployment-perhaps "package" is a bad word, after the Prime Minister spent so much time talking about its definition recently-I have no doubt at all that this measure will be of some help in giving more Canadians an opportunity to work. Even though this may be one advantage which flows from this particular legislation at this time, I think the legislation is desirable on its own merits and can stand on its own feet. If we were so fortunate as to have a full employment economy today it should be proceeded with even in those circumstances.
I would hope that the definition of the purposes for which this money may be used would be made quite clear, and that the definition will not include merely an extension or renovation of the premises of the given businessman who applies for a loan. The businessman who wants a loan to build a new building surely has as much claim to intermediate term credit as he would have if he wished to add a section to an existing building. I would hope it would be made clear that this money could be made available for the building of brand new premises and in fact could be used in connection with existing premises title to which is held by someone else. If that were done admittedly it would not bring about any additional employment opportunities, but surely it is a sufficiently good purpose that a businessman should have access to intermediate term credit for the purchase of an existing building if he feels that this is in his own business interest.
My first suggestion to the minister, therefore, is that the bill should make it clear that money will be made available to businessmen for the construction of new business premises 90205-6-6i
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses as well as for the purchase of existing premises when that appears to the businessman and banker involved to be a sound move. I think this would be in conformity with legislation which has as its chief purpose the providing of intermediate term credit to small businesses when such credit, as we all know, is not now readily available.
The second suggestion I have to make to the minister is that the interest rate should be 5 per cent. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act a fixed interest rate of 5 per cent is written in. Farmers and fishermen have obtained great advantage from this act over the years. An interest rate of 5 per cent is reasonable and fair, and money has been made available by the Canadian banking system at that rate. There is no doubt in my mind that a small businessman obtaining a loan is on a par with a farmer who obtains a loan; therefore the former should not be required to pay a higher rate of interest. A 5 per cent interest rate should be fixed in the bill that follows this resolution. A rate of 6 per cent should not be allowed. A 6 per cent rate is the maximum provided in the Bank Act.
The third suggestion I wish to make is that this guarantee should apply to credit unions and to the loans made to small businesses by credit unions as well as by banks. I ask the minister whether this was considered and whether any discussion has taken place with credit unions across Canada and their central organizations as to whether this course should be followed.
I am a strong supporter of the credit union movement. I think it is worth while for Canadians to be encouraged to save in a nonprofit, democratically operated organization such as a credit union. I can tell the minister that there are hundreds upon hundreds of communities across Canada where credit unions are providing an essential and valuable service that is not provided by banks. I believe that inquiry will show that small businesses in this country have had access to credit from credit unions in recent years. It has been almost impossible for small businessmen to obtain intermediate term credit through local banks because this is against banking practice.

I am sick and tired of having placed before this house by this government and by its predecessors good legislation

-which is good because it provides an avenue of credit for certain borrowers but which is inadequate because it discriminates against credit unions. Credit unions in many localities have been providing credit to small businessmen. When the bankers have said no, the credit unions have said yes. The government now comes forward with a guarantee and makes the guarantee applicable only to the banks. I say that is rank discrimination, and that this should be corrected. Credit unions are providing exceedingly good service in Canada. They are supported by Canadians all across our great land. They should have the support of the government in their worth-while endeavours by being placed on the same basis as the banks by way of guarantee under this legislation.
I have in my hand a publication entitled "Credit Unions in Canada", a report of the economic division of the Canadian Department of Agriculture for 1959. In that year it is reported that there were 4,566 credit unions in Canada with a huge membership of 2,347,317. There are many communities in our country where banks do not exist and banking facilities are not available, but which have credit unions. I suggest there is no solid reason why this legislation should not apply to credit unions.
I made the statement a little while ago that my understanding was that the Sherwood credit union, this very large credit union-I do not know whether it is the biggest but it is one of the biggest in Canada- charges a current rate of some 8 per cent. But there are certain advantages which obtain with respect to a loan from a credit union which usually do not obtain with respect to a loan from a bank. There is an insurance provision. If the person who has the loan should die, then the insurance wipes out the obligation so that the obligation is not one which the estate has to pay. I think it is ordinarily assumed that this particular insurance costs in the neighbourhood of 1 per cent.
The credit unions usually follow the policy of paying a much higher rate of interest on deposits than is paid by our chartered banks, so while their practices are somewhat different from those of the chartered banks, yet in my judgment they provide an excellent service and they should have the same guarantees that are given to banks.
The government has said that this measure is to help small business. In my opinion there is no better type of small business in our country than credit unions, and this legislation should be designed to assist in the development and expansion of credit unions and their facilities. I think the thousands

upon thousands of small business people across this country who have been doing business with credit unions and who have been getting credit facilities from their credit unions would welcome the inclusion of credit unions in this legislation by way of guarantee. If there were some administrative difficulties, I am sure the minister and his officials would be able to work out with credit unions across the country a method of bringing their loans under this kind of legislation.
It will be seen that without this kind of credit a very definite discrimination will be worked against credit unions. It means giving preference to the banks. The businessman can go to the bank, the bank can provide money, knowing that it has a government guarantee against 10 per cent of the aggregate. For the credit union there is no such guarantee.
Let us not fool ourselves into thinking that the banks will be undergoing any risk whatever with a guarantee of 10 per cent of the aggregate amount of the loan against loss. It means that it is absolutely impossible for the banks to incur the loss of a single dollar under this kind of legislation. The last time I looked at the figures I found that losses under the Farm Improvement Loans Act were running at, I believe three tenths of one per cent of the aggregate loans. The guarantee here is 10 per cent; therefore it is perfectly obvious that the banks are not undertaking any risk of any kind in doing this kind of business.
I make a plea to the minister that between now and the introduction of the bill, or certainly between now and the time the bill is discussed on second reading, he take all the steps that may be necessary to include credit unions in this legislation.

It is not very often that a person in public life has reason to feel satisfied, but when I heard His Excellency refer to loans to small business in the speech from the throne I felt very elated. I might also say that I am very proud to belong to the party whose government brings in this legislation.
For many years small business has been fighting an uphill battle. It has been very evident from all the briefs that have been presented to the government, from all the suggestions that have been made from all parts of this house for many years back, that this legislation has been required. Without being unkind, may I say that yesterday I heard the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo say that the idea was expressed by the Leader of the Opposition on February 1, 1958. At that time I felt that I should have liked to ask
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses him what the position of the Leader of the Opposition was on February 1, 1957 and February 1, 1956, and in the previous years, because I had heard statements that loans to small business had been requested for many years in the past. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam took us back as far as 1930, when loans to small businessmen had been requested in this house. Therefore, with this background, with all the urging that has been placed on this government since it came into office, and on previous governments, it is a great satisfaction to finally see this assistance to small business.
The present government came into office on a policy of aid to small business. This has not only been brought out by us many times; it was mentioned by members of the C.C.F. group yesterday. This is a fact. We did come in on this policy, and perhaps it might be said that it took three years to get around to putting it into effect. I think it took three years to clear up the underbrush of the past administration.

In order to keep up with the competition that is coming not only from other areas of North America but from	overseas as	well,
the tourist operator has to make general repairs and improvements. He has found himself unable to do all this work that is necessary because of the lack of credit facilities.

consideration to loans for the construction, improvement and repair of business premises and tourist operations.

The tourist industry is composed mainly of small businesses. While the few larger establishments, such as the hotels and lodges of the transportation companies, are well known, the greater percentage of restaurants and accommodation establishments are small. Many are family enterprises.
Most of Canada's hotels, resorts and camps are 30, 40 and 50 years old. At that time the rooms were much smaller and were not furnished as comfortably as the travelling public expect and demand today.
I will not read any more at that point, but on page 7 the association points out that one of the major deterrents to plant improvement is the lack of credit facilities. The production of these items will make work for the lumber camps and ultimately this will stimulate the Canadian economy. I believe it is clear, Mr. Chairman, that this measure will do a great deal to stimulate the type of winter employment that has been the aim of this government and that, in addition to the matters already mentioned by other speakers, Canada will get a lift out of the type of construction that will be made possible by this measure. Until we actually see the bill we cannot comment on the details. I think perhaps some of the comments

that have been made and questions asked may be answered when the bill is introduced.
For all these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to support the government in its presentation of this resolution.

I quite appreciate the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Laurier that we want to get on with this bill. The purpose I have in rising this afternoon is to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee a problem that perhaps pertains more to ridings like my own in metropolitan Toronto and other large cities. As we know, in the older areas we have a competition going on between the so-called ribbon strip type of merchandising and the shopping centres; and also, of course, between the corner stores and the chain stores.


One of the main difficulties arising in connection with the merchants in the older sections, in addition to that of being able to raise money to improve their premises so they can display their goods to better advantage, is the matter of parking. That perhaps has been one of the reasons for the development of the shopping centres. I refer to this method of being able to collect stores together and provide adequate parking facilities. I welcome the intention of the government to continue its assistance to small business and to translate promises into action. However, I am wondering whether the interpretation of the act would be broad enough to provide that a number of merchants could borrow money in an effort to get together in providing parking lots adjacent to their premises, something which is a form of improvement to their premises. In certain sections of older cities, as I know is the case in Toronto, merchants would not be anxious to put too much money into the improvement of premises until they could be assured that would-be shoppers had the opportunity of parking near their premises.
Another question, Mr. Chairman, would be related to the fact that some merchants in these older sections would like to move out into newer sections. Would this act permit them to obtain loans to make this move? It may be that under their present circumstances business has not been so good; sales in certain areas have been going down, shall we say, and they feel that they would like to move out of a particular area but cannot afford to do so. Would loans cover the moving from one premises to another, and improving the new premises? Those are the two main points that I wish to bring to the attention of the house.
I know that in respect to parking the government has assisted, through the winter works program, by paying one half of the labour costs to cities that have applied for assistance in that respect. But I suggest that this is not sufficient, because the major cost in obtaining parking lots is the expropriation of property which is necessary to secure these lots. I hope the government will review that situation and give assistance in the older sections in the form of loans to parking authorities to make parking facilities available in those areas. I know this is a municipal matter, but when we are taking this over-all view in assisting merchants, it seems to me unreasonable to provide an opportunity for them to improve their premises without providing facilities for customers to park and then come and look at their premises.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to add my thanks to the Minister of Finance and the government

for recognizing these problems of the small businessman and merchant, and I add my support to the measure.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is with
pleasure that I rise to speak on this resolution, primarily because it is the first measure of its kind in Canada's history that recognizes the small retailer and, second, because it will be of immeasurable benefit to many small business establishments in my riding. The very wording of this resolution is indicative of the consideration given by this administration to the average citizen engaged in independent free enterprise.
There are some who will question this measure and ask why it was necessary. Generally speaking, a small business is one with a limited investment that is independently owned or employing a limited number of people with relatively small sales.
What is the problem of the small business? In recent years competition has become increasingly keen owing to the activities of the large corporate chains and the supermarkets, which rely on their ability to draw customers from a larger area than their own communities. Moreover, supermarket locations are not usually available to small business, due to their financial standing, as their lease of premises is of little help as security for initial bond issues. However, independent stores are a necessity to round out retail sales in shopping centres. To survive, small business concerns therefore need capital for modernization to keep pace with the times.
When you have the limited financial resources which I have just outlined, you cannot borrow long term money from the public or other sources. The matter is an immediate problem, however, which cannot wait until enough money is secured, or set aside, from the profits. The present movement is too rapid to permit this.
What small business needs, therefore, is a plan under which an approved risk can borrow money, repayable on extended terms. At best, banking accommodation, though substantial, has been of a more temporary nature, and the fact is that suppliers, generally speaking, can do no more than render assistance in carrying inventories and receivables. Long term loans have rarely been made available to the average retailer.
The need for extended credit is not something new in our economy: it has been recognized before by governments in various forms. For instance, under some form of guarantee there are the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, home improvement loans and others which I could mention.
I realize that in the provinces of Alberta, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland some form of financial assistance is

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses available but it does, in the main, pertain to primary industries such as agriculture, fishing and mining. These loans or guarantees are generally first mortgage loans and in the aggregate they have not been large. I believe the experience of loans under these forms of guarantee has been in the main satisfactory. This established procedure therefore sets a pattern for assistance to small business and enables this program to be established on sound business lines with a minimum of delay.
The importance of the small businessman in the national economy is, I think, clearly recognized in all government circles. As has been previously mentioned by other speakers, the industrial development bank was established in 1944 for the purpose of assisting certain small businesses. Unfortunately, however, the administration setting up the industrial development bank did not at that time show any concern for the welfare of the small retailer, for no provision was made for assistance to him.
It is a generally conceded fact that unless the independent retailer can be kept in a reasonably competitive position with the corporate chains it naturally follows that he will go out of business. Throughout the years some wholesale firms, in an effort to keep retailers competitive, have established a service to retailers department. Through this department they give expert advice to retailers in connection with store planning, arrangement of merchandise in the store, and in general what could be summed up as merchandising policy. However, increasing modernization programs demand larger sums of money as chain store competitors have grown in size and range of merchandise, and the independent retailer must follow suit if he hopes to maintain his position. Unfortunately, to date, many aggressive and capable merchants are not in a position financially to remodel or extend their premises, or build new buildings nor are they in a position to finance the necessary new equipment required by a remodelling program.
For this reason I welcome this resolution by the Minister of Finance who, in my opinion, is one of the most capable finance ministers in Canada's history. According to his statement this measure when approved will assist four classes of business-manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade and service. As this includes the tourist industry I believe any enterprising Canadian businessman will experience little difficulty in financing his business expansion. Needless to say, the tourist industry is of vital importance to my riding and to Nova Scotia which we call Canada's ocean playground,

and I know there are many in the tourist industry who will take advantage of this type of assistance to improve their present facilities.
It has often been said this is Canada's century. Under the great national development program planned by this government new areas will be opened up for settlement by new Canadians. It is a well known fact that in areas with a population of 1,000 or less there is little to attract the chain store operator. It is in these areas that the independent retailer fills a worth-while need. However, he must still compete with the mail order houses and this measure will enable him to finance the most modern equipment and operate his business at the lowest possible expense.
Finally, when we consider the 1 events that have occurred in Cuba and South Africa, where businesses large and small have been confiscated by the government, or taken over by revolution and revolt, only then do we realize the tremendous opportunity open to businessmen in Canada. In promoting small business we are on safe ground. Under stable government and sound leadership there is a security to business investment in this nation that is not paralleled anywhere else in the world. For these reasons I commend the Minister of Finance on this resolution and hope that it finds ready acceptance among all members of the house.

I assure you, Mr. Chairman, as well as the hon. member for Laurier, that I shall be brief in my remarks. However, I wish to comment on this particular measure. Certainly the Minister of Finance and the government deserve the commendation of all hon. members and, indeed, of every citizen of Canada for introducing this particular proposal.
It is quite evident from the views which have been put forward already that there is a broad understanding of the necessity for this measure. It is also interesting to note that the proposal has been put forward not only by the Minister of Finance but, long before this time, by other people who have promoted it, apparently, for years and years. However that may be, I certainly compliment the Minister of Finance and the government upon bringing it to fruition. It does not matter to me if members of other parties are anxious to get on the band wagon. I do not believe this will be a very contentious piece of legislation and we will all be very happy to see it made effective.
The restrictions which were placed on the money supply as early as 1955 caused a great deal of concern to small businessmen in this country and certainly from then until the present time it has also, probably, caused

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses
embarrassment to some of these people. I feel very strongly on this point, because I feel at times that the chartered banks have been responsible in no small measure for the way in which credit facilities have been handled in the past in that they were not sufficiently generous in supporting this particular phase of our economy. It is gratifying, nevertheless, to hear of the co-operation of these institutions and to hear that they hail it as an excellent measure.
As a result of this resolution the pressure of corporate organizations on small business will be removed to some degree and the independence of those individuals who have made such a worthy contribution to community life in Canada will be restored. I refer of course, as did the hon. member for Davenport, to the retail sector of our economy in particular to which this measure will apply. I have no doubt as to the benefit that will accrue to smaller branches of industry as well as to other phases of the economy, but my remarks will in particular refer to retail business.
The competition in this particular field which is presented by corporate chains has become, I think we can reasonably say, ruthless. The small businessman is feeling this pressure from day to day. When we make the comparison with the unwritten law of ethics that existed among small businessmen this is a very disturbing factor in that part of the distribution system. We must remember that all of these businessmen are true Canadians. They are in our distribution system the best of Canadians. They are that particular segment of the economy that will foster secondary industry, that will put Canadian goods before the public, that will make a concerted effort to sell Canadian goods to the citizens of this country.
Certainly it would be a very simple matter for me to prove to the committee that the small chains as well as the larger chain stores are not too particular in this case because the imports that are causing concern to Canadian secondary industry are being presented, displayed and sold in large quantities by those stores. The small businessman is the man who promotes the welfare of our secondary industry.
In this regard I have had numerous conversations in the last couple of weeks with people interested in this question as well as with those who are participating in this type of distribution of imports. It has been said that I am nationalistic in my views in this case. I did not want to mention the fact that I am in the retail business, but I can assure hon. members that if this is Canadian nationalism I intend to support and promote
it because the presentation of the manufactured goods of Canadian secondary industry is the only way we can get it across to our people. After all, it is the people themselves who will create a market whether for our products or for imported products.
I fear that the day has passed when a businessman's integrity in the community and his own character are used as the basis upon which he can approach a bank for credit facilities. I compliment the minister in recognizing this principle which I think is basic in the outline of the resolution that has been proposed.
I feel as many others do that possibly business in Canada is becoming too dependent on the state for its support but as the hon. member for Kootenay West said last evening we must be aware of certain monolithic powers that are becoming apparent in our Canada. If the end result of the resolution is to create legislation that takes cognizance of these matters then certainly it is a worth-while proposal.
When you, Mr. Chairman, or some other hon. member of the committee participated in the debate the thought was expressed that some value would flow from improving the aesthetic appearance of the business section of small communities. I believe that is true. In many instances visitors will assess the progress and prosperity of a town on the basis of its appearance and the impressions they receive while travelling through its business section. Unquestionably this measure will be of assistance to people in improving the appearance of their establishments and in attracting customers for the sale of the goods to which I referred.
This segment of our business community has been clearly defined by the minister and although the definition does not include some of the factors mentioned by some who have spoken in this debate this remains a worthwhile and notable measure. In my opinion it represents the most imaginative step on behalf of this sector of the business community ever taken by any government in this country. I am pleased to be able to heartily support this measure in every way.

Mr. Chairman, we have had another dissertation on gloom and doom from the hon. member for Skeena. I do not intend to say very much on this measure, but there are one or two points that I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister.
First of all, I should like to say to the hon. member for Skeena that he is not aware of what the small businessman is thinking about if, one, he thinks that he is not in favour of the changes we made in the Combines Investigation Act at the last session; and, two, if he thinks they are worried about what this government is doing. They are more worried about the inroads of the creeping socialism that is taking place in Canada than anything else.
I want to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that if this legislation is to be as effective as we would like it to be the challenge will be to the banks of this country. It is because of my knowledge of the workings of the Farm Improvement Loans Act that I bring this to the attention of the minister. There have been occasions, particularly in western Canada, when we have felt that the banks have fallen down on this challenge even though their loans were guaranteed. Sometimes it has seemed to us that
the very time when the banks had fallen down on this challenge were the times when we had crop failures or other climatic disasters, the very time when the farmers could have used the money. At those times the banks failed miserably in providing loans through the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This happened not long ago in our particular part of the country.
On occasion in western Canada we also feel that the head offices of some of our banks are a little bit too far away from us, and it becomes too easy for the local manager to say, "Well, I am sorry; head office says no". It is this sort of thing that is of particular importance to our small businessmen. They will appreciate this particular legislation. However, I repeat to the banks, the challenge is theirs. This is their opportunity to prove that they can and will co-operate in providing a free enterprise economy with the credit which is needed because if they fail on this occasion they may not get another chance to provide guaranteed loans to our people and the government will be in the lending business directly.
I also wish to point out to my socialist friends that there is not very much difference between some of the large monopolies and government monopolies. In both instances the consumer is the loser. We have seen this here. Many of us who have lived in some of the residential areas of Ottawa in which the grocery or the food market is controlled by one of the large chain stores know that because of unfair zoning regulations, which we now have in most of our cities, the small businessman, the small grocer, is crowded out of those shopping centres and, as a result, the consumer has to pay more for his food. This is something that this legislation can help to correct, but we will need the cooperation of the banks and of our municipal governments in their zoning regulations to make it as effective as it can be made.
I do not think there is any doubt at all that this legislation will provide an innumerable number of jobs for working people right across Canada. I commend the minister and the government on the legislation.

Mr. Chairman, as a small business operator, I wish to associate myself with the other hon. members who have complimented the Minister of Finance upon the measure he has brought before the house. I should like to have seen it go a little further than the resolution appears to go. However, there are several points in the resolution on Which I would appreciate more clarification.
In his introductory remarks the minister said that the bill to be founded upon the present resolution deals with the provision of intermediate term credit to small business. In my opinion, the use to which the credit can be put is very limited in scope, and I suppose that was one of the purposes of this measure. The resolution states that the use of the credit is limited to the improvement and modernization of premises and equipment. No provision is made for the inclusion of operating or working capital or capital to consolidate liabilities. As I said before, I presume that was purposely omitted from this measure.
If a proprietor rents his premises rather than owns them his use of the intermediate term credit is more or less restricted to the purchase of equipment. It would seem to me that the term "equipment" in this case is more applicable to small manufacturing businesses than it is to the other three categories, that is wholesale, retail or services. I should like to ask the minister, is the definition of the term "equipment" going to be so broad as to include increases in inventory in the case of wholesalers or retail outlets? In so far as service businesses are concerned, would an enterprise conducted by a professional person such as a doctor, dentist and so on, be included?
Then I have another thought in relation to the figure of $250,000 which sets the limit on a small business. Under this resolution, the maximum amount of money that may be


borrowed is $25,000. Is this maximum amount based upon 10 per cent of the gross revenue of any one firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext: No.

speechtext: It is just a coincidence, then, is it, that the definition of a small business mentions the gross revenue of $250,000 and the maximum amount of the loan is 10 per cent of that?

speechtext: I gave the reasons for the selection of $250,000 as the basis for the definition of a small business as applied to the gross revenue of the business. The maximum loan permissible under this measure is $25,000. There is no direct relationship between the $25,000 and the $250,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
The comparison there is 10 per cent, is it not?
Another point I wish to mention concerns the regulations that will eventually be issued under this measure. How broad will those regulations be? I have in mind some of the other measures with which we have dealt during past sessions. One of these would be the Civil Service Act. Under the Civil Service Act, I understand that one and a quarter days is allowed to each employee for each month worked. This seems very simple. It means that for each month worked he is entitled to one and a quarter days holidays up to a maximum of 15 days in any one year. However, a treasury board minute has been passed which states that no employee is entitled to holidays during the first six months of his employment. The regulations, therefore, are much stronger than the act. I trust that the minister will guard against such regulations being enacted under this measure.
Then again, last year, we were mentioning the Farm Credit Act. The purpose to which loans obtained under this act may be put is set out in the act. It is presumed that anyone who can qualify and who wants to use money under the terms laid down in this act can do so. However, in practice that seems not to be the case. Perhaps the hon. member for Skeena, who was so critical of members talking on this bill, could explain why, in the regulations issued under the Farm Credit Act, regulation 12 (2) says this: Where, in the Judgment of the corporation, an applicant for a loan has the resources required to complete an economic farm unit the corporation may decline to make a loan to him or limit the amount of the loan to be made to him.
In other words, under this act there has to be a certain amount of security available before the applicant is entitled to a loan, but in some other cases the board or the bureaucrats, if you wish to call them that, who control this act may determine who

can obtain a loan. I have had some cases in which the assets were considered to be too high and the applicants have been refused on that ground. I hope the same situation will not apply in the case of these loans to small businesses.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this debate has been a most interesting one for many reasons, chief of which may be the fact that this measure has inspired opposition groups to fall all over each other in attempting to claim authorship of this important and timely piece of legislation. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo must surely recognize how pitiful it was to try to tie this act to the leader of his party. A Pearson plan there may have been, but the Liberal party certainly never had a plan to help small business. That record is one I should like to touch upon later.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the other C.C.F. speakers have not much faith in the small businessmen of this country or they would not question their integrity by referring to these men taking out loans they would be unable to repay. The outstanding record of Canadian farmers with regard to loans from the banks, farm improvement loans, and so on, leads me to believe that the hon. members should have more confidence in the small businessmen of this country. I believe they will prove to be as equally alert and industrious in undertaking and fulfilling their financial obligations as have the farm people.
If you study the history of small business you cannot escape the conclusion that it is the history of Canada as well. It is perhaps the greatest denominator in our economy. It is one of the pivots upon which development in Canada has depended. There is no more romantic chapter in the history of this country. It is a story of achievement, continued development and community building which, generally, is not fully appreciated. Indeed it would almost appear as though the only time governments in the past have remembered small business was when they imposed taxation or required someone to collect taxes. It is refreshing to note that this government has recognized the vitality of this segment of our economy by introducing this measure which should multiply the effective benefits of small business in every part of the nation.
The role played by small busines is apparent everywhere you go in Canada. I see it everywhere in my own riding, which is an agricultural community, and I can think of scores of towns in the Rosthern constituency in which small businessmen by their foresight and planning, have made those towns stand out from their neighbouring communities. Every time I meet these businessmen I see mirrored in their eyes the future of their communities and the future of Canada as well. They are the real builders of this nation, providing our people with services and leaving to future generations those valuable principles of service and courtesy that singled them out as leaders in their respective communities.
I saw this many times as I visited along the St. Lawrence river and the cities of Montreal, Toronto and Quebec; and it was brought to my attention much more forcibly where the textile industry had been brought to a halt during the past decade. I saw it in the eyes of a taxi driver in the city of Halifax. I saw it in the shops and buildings wherever I went in the maritimes. Doors were barred, windows were boarded up; this was undeniable evidence of the failure of Liberalism in its administration and responsibility in so far as the spirit of confederation was concerned in the great Atlantic region. When I looked at those buildings I knew that they represented, perhaps more than anything else, the utter decay of Liberalism in this country as an active political force. Mr. Chairman, they seemed to be much more than that; they seemed to be like lighthouses alert against the perils and corrosive forces and influences that had over a long period of years robbed the people of this area of their true heritage, namely the promise and vision of confederation.
If I might be permitted to say so, I think the fisherman is a small businessman too. When I looked at the rotting hulks of vessels that had once been proud to claim Canada's fisheries as a thriving and a living industry, I could not help but think of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the hon. member for Essex East and the rest of that played-out school of herring, caught and entangled in the web of their own administrative neglect during their period of office.
As I moved across the prairies during the past several years I saw the unfulfilled hopes of implement agents and others written in the story of the padlocks and boards that proclaimed "closed" in a measure that cannot help but touch the heart of anyone who understands the sacrifice that small businessmen make to play a part in their communities.

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses
In my own riding the machinery agent and the automobile agent is indispensable. He is the one who introduces new machines that cut costs and increase efficiency. He must provide the plant to service the machinery he sells. He must have the room lor stock and inventory that he must carry in order to service those machines. He must maintain offices and equipment lor the staff to keep accurate records for himself, for his customers and for the company with which he deals as well as for governmental agencies. These things require more capital than the average small businessman has at the time when he needs it most. Other businesses are in like position, whether concerned with groceries, drugs, hardware or any of the other numerous services required in the community.
This measure brought forward by this government should be of great assistance to many of those engaged in small business. During the past several years, a period ol time when we had a Liberal administration that neglected to provide the small businessman with encouragement, people in many parts of this nation found it necessary to get together on a self-help basis and form co-operative organizations in order to provide for themselves those things which businessmen were unable to provide for them under the conditions that existed. Those co-operatives have served a useful purpose and there is no doubt that they will continue to do so in those places where local businessmen are unable to give the service that the people of that local area require. They are also an excellent training ground for people who go into service in those respective areas.
The department of co-operatives in the province of Saskatchewan is doing a fair job. However, the socialist and C.C.F. government of the province of Saskatchewan have never been known as being friendly to small businessmen. Indeed, the only time when they recognized the small businessman was when they raised the 2 per cent education tax to 3 per cent and asked him to collect it. That was a tax that they had pledged themselves to remove prior to their election in 1944. The mortality rate for small business in Saskatchewan has been terrific under C.C.F. administration. It is, of course, interesting to note that for the greater part of this decade we had a Liberal government at Ottawa.
For these many reasons I am therefore pleased to congratulate the Minister of Finance for bringing forward this measure. This measure should help to build the sturdier, more productive business and industrial plant that is the challenge of our day and generation. I

should like to congratulate the Prime Minister and the ministry as a whole upon the implementation of this pledge which was given to the people of Canada as part of our program to be brought forward during the life of the present parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to express my views at too great length on this matter, because I would not want to delay the work which started so well and has been facilitated by the co-operation we have had from the hon. members of the opposition since the beginning of this session. However, I would like to make a few remarks on the financial assistance which the government proposes to extend to small businesses, that is to the owners of small establishments, as indicated in the resolution now being discussed.
When the speech from the throne opening the first session of the twenty fourth parliament in 1958 was read out, the Conservative government announced the formation of an advisory committee to help small businesses or supply smaller establishments with the technical advice they might need with regard to organization. Thus the concept had been launched, which will take form today, thanks to the bill which is to be submitted shortly in order to ensure, by means of a guarantee, loans made by banks to small businessmen for the improvement and modernization of their equipment and premises, as indeed, announced in the resolution now before us.
This bill will greatly help business and our secondary industries in the more remote parts of this country, like the district I have the honour to represent here in this house.
I do not propose to repeat all the points raised on this matter by the previous speakers who, indeed, were on the whole, unanimous in tendering their congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), as well as to the Conservative government introducing this legislation.
Apart from the help it will bring to small industries of which quite a few belong to my fellow citizens in the fine province of Quebec, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) stated yesterday that such help would also be available to the tourist industry. Now that is a very important point for the northwestern part of Quebec, where the tourist industry is just starting to be of any value, more particularly since several of our highways leading into Montreal have been paved. Besides, the Abitibi highway system will be completely paved within a few years. On previous occasions, the senior and junior chambers of commerce in my district more particularly discussed the question of the tourist

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses
industry and brought forward a number of suggestions and resolutions in this respect. I would more particularly like to mention the junior chamber of commerce in my district, which prepared an excellent tourist guidebook a few years ago, so that the northwestern part of Quebec would be better known. Anyway, two years ago I took great pleasure in distributing those guidebooks to all members of this house and those of the other place. The publication was bilingual and, besides giving the historical background of our towns and a summary of the history of the Abitibi, it contained a most interesting tourist map.
With the assistance that will be provided to the tourist industry through the act about to be submitted, I hope that improved facilities as well as new commodities will be available and that members and senators who visit my part of the country, as I sincerely hope they will, shall find their stay all the more pleasant.
When presenting this resolution yesterday, the Minister of Finance indicated that the loans will also be available to co-operatives. May I congratulate him on that point. Loans of that kind are already available under the agricultural legislation for the benefit of cooperatives.
Another important point raised by the leader of the C.C.F. group, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), is that of credit unions.
Under the legislation that the Conservative government is planning to bring down in order to assist the smaller branches of industry, it was pointed out that in some districts of this country interest rates charged by credit unions run as high as 12 per cent. May I say that, as far as Abitibi and northwestern Quebec is concerned, credit unions lend money at 6 per cent. This I know from personal experience, as I am a member of the supervisory committee of the western Quebec credit union (caisse centrale Desjardins). I had an opportunity of seeing the organization at work for several years. To my mind credit unions, as pointed out by several other members, render important services, operating as they do in the smaller communities where banks have no branches.
Banks, of course, operate under federal legislation, and the federal government provides for regular inspections of their operations, whereas credit unions are under provincial jurisdiction-I am now referring to what
is called caisses populaires in French localities. I wonder if the Minister of Finance should not get in touch with provincial anthorities in order to reach an agreement in this regard and make it possible for credit unions to lend money as the banks will be authorized to do under this act. This might require an amendment to the Bank Act or an agreement with the provincial governments concerned. But this is only a suggestion. There is no doubt that the caisses populaires, which have already rendered services to their members, will be called upon to render other services in the future. It would be a good thing, I think, if they were allowed to benefit by the bill which will be introduced following the present resolution.
