speechtext:
I trust that hon. members of the house will indulge me if I read the technical part of the statement I have to make. I do not like having to do it, but this is a complicated bill.
Since early in 1957 Canada has built half a million houses. Two million persons are now living in this new housing accommodation. In other words, one ninth of the population, men, women and children are living in new accommodation built in the last four years. In this step forward the federal government, through its housing policy, has played a very significant role, indeed, a dominant one. From 1957 until now National Housing Acts loans were approved for 225,000 new dwellings. Nearly half of these came directly from the government itself through its agent the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Since September, 1957 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, expanding beyond its old frontiers, has been making loans in all parts of the country, not merely in small towns, as it had hitherto done.
Most of the corporation's loans have been to home owners but it has substantially increased its rental loans to limited dividend projects intended for low income families and old people. For them some 15,000 loans were made.
Home owner loans accounted for about
35,000	of the total of C.M.H.C. loans from 1957 to the present date. At the moment any home owner anywhere in Canada, with any income, can get a housing loan from C.M.H.C. if none is available to him from a bank or other approved lender. I ask hon. members to note that particularly. Loans by C.M.H.C. to builders from 1957 to date have been approved in respect of some 50,000 units.
Taking all C.M.H.C. loans into account from 1957 through 1960, that is to say, loans to limited dividend companies, other rental entrepreneurs, home owners and builders, a total amount of $1.1 billion has been committed, accounting for 108,000 new dwelling units. The scale of this lending policy more than any other single thing represents the main contribution of this government to
National Housing Act
housing over the past three and one half years and the main departure from earlier policies.
The lending program was pursued with the basic aim of increasing house building in Canada in order to improve housing conditions in the country. The policy, especially on builders' loans, also served another important purpose

the support of winter employment, and in its application the government took special pains to direct its assistance as far as possible toward the lower income range of eligible N.H.A. borrowers.
This endeavour of the government resulting in over 100,000 houses in three and one half years for people of modest incomes should be seen in the perspective of another 125,000 built under the act with insured loans by approved lenders. In other words, the government insured the approved loans. About a quarter of a million other houses were built outside the terms of the act at the same time. These latter, built with private funds, were largely for families with more substantial incomes and bring the total, as I said a moment ago, to the half million new houses.
Against this background I should like to comment on housing developments in the year just coming to a close. There will probably be about 110,000 new housing starts. I say that for the benefit of my hon. friends opposite. There will probably be about 110,000 starts in 1960 and something over 120,000 completions. This will represent a decline of 22 per cent in starts and 15 per cent in completions as compared with the 1959 program.
Some hon. members will recall-as will the hon. member over there who is smiling- that about a year ago in assessing the house building prospects for 1960 I did warn of a likely decline in the number of new starts. More hon. members will recall, however, that my declared expectation was 125,000 starts, rather than 110,000. I mention this for the benefit of those hon. members who may have allowed my prediction to slip from memory, so that everyone in the house may be equally possessed' of this incriminating piece of information. In the church, as all hon. members know, one may lay just claim to the office of minister without exemplifying the rare gifts and attainments that are proper to the role of prophet. I trust that hon. members will allow me the same latitude in this place.
For the first time since the war the demand for housing has become a limiting factor. Generally throughout the fifties the demand for N.H.A. loans was strong enough to use up available supplies of funds. Beginning in the fall of 1957, as I have mentioned earlier, private funds under the N.H.A.

National Housing Act
were supplemented by government funds on a major scale. The application of these funds enabled the house building industry to maintain a high output from the fall of 1957 to the end of 1959. It seemed likely, in view of the rates of building achieved in this period, that the excess demand for N.H.A. funds would not last indefinitely and that soon or later a time would be reached when substantial increases in house building could not be brought about merely by making funds available on the existing terms, although much could be achieved by improving the terms.
A year ago, however, there was no clear evidence that demand was weaker. The decline in house building forecast at that time was based on the definite expectation that there would be less mortgage money available under the act in 1960 than in 1959. The banks had virtually stopped mortgage lending because other investments were more attractive to them. It was known that the amount of government lending in the year ahead would be substantially curtailed. Lending by the life, loan and trust companies under the act was then close to a standstill.
I remember being tremendously worried about this. It was one of the first things I encountered when I became minister. These lenders were brought back into the fold by the increase in the insured mortgage interest rate from 6 per cent to 6f per cent which took place last December. The banks were unable to take advantage of this higher rate and the change had no effect of course on the expected participation by C.M.H.C. whose lending is governed by policy considerations rather than yield.
However, the decline in N.H.A. mortgage lending by C.M.H.C. and the banks does not wholly explain the fall-off in starts in 1960. Demand was also cut off. There was a distinct easing in the supply of mortgage money at mid-year but we did not immediately get a corresponding increase in mortgage loan approvals. Although the flow of insured loans has now gone up, the total for the year is still down. Activity under direct C.M.H.C. lending programs was also falling short of expectations. As is to be expected in this kind of situation there were still some builders and some prospective owners in some areas who were unable to get mortgage loans and it was primarily to meet these special demands that C.M.H.C. direct lending policy was eased over the past few months.
Hon. members will recall that the original intention for 1960 was to keep direct C.M.H.C. lending commitments within $175 million which meant about 18,000 dwelling units. This required a more restrictive policy in

the allocation of C.M.H.C. loans than had been applied in 1959 and in the previous two years. Aside from limited dividend projects, the initial policy established in April was for loans to home owners only, and those only with incomes below $5,600. In July it was announced that as from September 1, loans for borrowers with incomes of up to $7,600 would be available and that builders could have loans for dwellings whose purchasers, also subject to the $7,600 income limit, were on hand.
Market conditions at this time, however, cautioned against the provision of speculative loans to builders. Early in October the income limits were removed altogether and by the time the year is over C.M.H.C. will have committed loans for about 18,000 units all together, representing an amount of $175 million. While this result is close to the target set early in the present year it required a less restrictive lending policy throughout the year than we had originally expected because of demand weakness. As hon. members know we did not anticipate the weakness in demand which transpired around the beginning of June. Fortunately the means to strengthen demand are at our disposal. Amendments to the National Housing Act are now proposed which will, among other things, increase the size of insured loans that N.H.A. borrowers can obtain.
Having given the background, let me now deal with the substance of what the proposed legislation proposes. This will lower down payments, thereby admitting new borrowers to the active market.
Hon. members will recall that when this government came to office we found that the equity or down payment requirement for home ownership loans was so high that a very large proportion of Canadian families were unable to take advantage of the N.H.A. to acquire a home. At that time the maximum size of insured loans under the act was set at 90 per cent of the first $8,000 of lending value and 70 per cent of the remainder. In December of 1957 we amended the act to provide a loan of 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value and 70 per cent of the remainder. This change had the effect of permitting large numbers of lower income families to enter the market. I may say that the guiding rule of this government has been to assist the little man to own his own home. This government has always considered it desirable to do its utmost to assist borrowers at the lower end of the eligible income range. We have watched the situation carefully during the past three years and it has become evident that a further reduction in down payment would enable many more Canadian families to buy a home.

As will be shown in the bill we therefore propose to change the ratio from 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value to 95 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value and 70 per cent of the remainder, as before. This relates to the lending value as distinguished from the purchase price. This change will have the effect of increasing the loan and reducing the down payment for a house worth $10,000 by $500; for a house worth $11,000 by $550; and for houses worth $12,000 to $14,000 by $600. It will have no effect on houses worth more than $14,857.
As hon. members can see this is designed to help the little man. I might add that there are many Canadian families who have the income to make the payments on these houses but who are unable to get together the initial amount to make a down payment. As hon. members are aware the initial down payment is usually very substantial when one considers the other expenditures that have to be taken into account in connection with the purchase of a dwelling.
While this government has always been concerned with the problem of lower income families, it is important to recognize that at least half of the N.H.A. demand is for dwellings worth $14,000 and up. The N.H.A. maximum loan by regulation for single family dwellings has remained at $12,800 since 1954. During this period construction costs have risen substantially, and higher construction costs have caused down payments on houses worth more than $14,000 to increase. The cost of housing and property has gone up by at least 20 per cent, I would say.
Higher down payments have made more N.H.A. borrowers resort to second mortgages at high rates of interest or other forms of secondary financing to accumulate the necessary down payments. This year approximately 20 per cent of N.H.A. borrowers had to make use of second mortgages to accumulate the necessary equity. Hon. members know what disaster can sometimes overtake people when they become involved in second mortgages. It is considered necessary, therefore, to raise the maximum loan set by regulation. It is proposed to change the present maximum loan from $12,800 to $14,200 for single family dwellings with three bedrooms or less-that is our standard house-and to $14,900 for larger dwellings.
There will be corresponding changes in maximum loans for other structural types of dwellings. This change will have the effect of increasing the loan and reducing the down payments on houses worth $15,000 by $700 and for houses worth $16,000 and up by $1,400. We believe that this increase in loan will go a long way toward helping potential home owners to accumulate the necessary
National Housing Act
equity and reduce the incidence of secondary financing at onerous terms for some borrowers.
The combined effect of these two changes will reduce down payments for a broad range of N.H.A. borrowers. The higher loans will of course increase monthly payments of principal and interest on N.H.A. mortgages. In order to make it possible for lenders to reduce monthly charges, it is proposed to amend the act to extend the permissible repayment term from the present 30-year maximum to 35 years. That does not mean that a person is compelled to do that, but if he requires it he can get the 35-year maximum. For example, an increase of $600 in a $12,000 loan at 30 years will raise monthly payment charges by $3.85. To offset this an extension in the repayment period from 30 years to 35 years will reduce monthly charges on a $12,600 loan by $3.47.
On rental housing-this is very important -the act now authorizes loans of 80 per cent of the lending value. To keep rental demand in step with home ownership building, it is proposed to raise this 80 per cent ratio to 85 per cent. Similarly, there will be adjustments to the maximum loan amounts authorized by regulation for the various structural types of dwellings built for rental purposes, such as row houses, apartments, duplexes and triplexes.
These changes in the act and in the regulations are being put forward at this time to support demand along a broad front. It has been suggested by some that demand could be stimulated by a lowering of the interest rate as well. So it could, but in the present market a lower interest rate would reduce the amount of private lending under the act, and place heavier pressure on the federal government to meet the increased demand for loans. Even today, with the moderation in the pressure of demand which I have already mentioned, the federal government through C.M.H.C. is still carrying a large part of the lending load and hon. members will keep in mind that we are just residual lenders; we make no direct loans unless the borrower has been refused by a bank or by another approved lender. It is no part of our intention to increase the demand for housing funds and at the same time kill the incentive of private lenders to supply as much of the funds as possible. Again I cannot forget the way in which the funds dried up toward the end of 1959, when an interest rate of 6 per cent became totally unrealistic and when the borrowers turned in droves and in the thousands to the government to help them out of their dilemma.
This stimulus to demand, brought about bj higher loans, will of course have very definite

National Housing Act
implications for government lending policy as well. It may be that the supply of private funds from the life insurance, loan and trust companies, and from the banks also in time, will be sufficient to meet the increase in demand resulting from this legislation. This is my hope and I should like to say how happy I am that each week the participation of the life insurance companies and the mortgage companies increases over the corresponding week last year. They are really in the market in a big way in an effort to make up for the withdrawal of the banks from the market. Although this is my hope, you may rest assured that this government is not proposing changes to increase demand merely to see it bottled up in the future for want of private funds. This government will not stand idly by in such a situation any more than it has stood idly by in the past. The purpose of this legislation is to permit the continued improvement of housing conditions in Canada and to contribute to the pace of general economic activity. We will not see these purposes frustrated for lack of private mortgage funds. If the present lending institutions cannot provide adequate mortgage funds we shall seek other means to broaden the base of private lending or to enable the federal government to continue its major role as a mortgage lender; but we hope that private funds will be available.
The proposed changes in legislation also offer wider aids to urban redevelopment; public housing and home improvement. Virtually every major city has recently examined its obsolete housing by carrying out an urban renewal study. Only two major cities have not, Edmonton and Calgary, and of course they are in the position of being almost new cities and they may not need it at the present time. This government has encouraged this activity by offering grants of up to 75 per cent of the cost. These studies have enabled our cities to identify the worst areas of blight and to establish priorities for redeveloping these run-down areas. During the past three years this government has approved slum clearance projects for the redevelopment of over 300 acres of blight in Canadian cities. The total cost of acquisition and clearance is estimated to be more than $22 million, and federal contributions of over $11 million have been approved. Projects are currently under way in Halifax, Saint John, New Brunswick, Montreal, Toronto, Windsor, Sarnia and Vancouver.
Many other cities are studying their own special problems and will soon be anxious to secure financial assistance for redevelopment projects. It is the intention of this government to consider all worthy applications and we stand ready to make contributions of

one half the cost of acquisition and clearance in such projects. In order that this growing program should not be impeded we propose to increase that statutory limit for federal contributions under section 23 of the National Housing Act from $25 million to $50 million.
The many urban renewal studies-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I outline the plans of the government I should like all hon. members to keep in mind the fact that every one of these plans represent a tremendous amount of employment. I should have referred to that fact at the beginning of my remarks, but I would ask hon. members to keep in mind the potentialities.
We were talking about urban renewal studies at the dinner hour, and these studies have revealed something which is new and something to which I would direct the attention of this house. I refer to the fact that there are very few housing areas that are so run down or so plainly needed for other purposes that massive and complete clearance is necessary. In other words, the blighted areas approved for redevelopment do not all require complete demolition and many potential urban renewal areas contain housing accommodation with many years of useful life which could be rehabilitated and used for lower income families. As I have reiterated many times, we are interested primarily in the little man. If we can provide for him adequate accommodation at lower cost than new housing, so much the better.
Section 36 of the National Housing Act enables the federal government to undertake jointly with the government of any province projects for the construction of new housing for rent, but does not make provision for the acquisition of suitable existing housing in urban renewal areas. This deficiency in the public housing provisions of the act makes area-wide rehabilitation difficult, and consequently cities tend to wait for severe blight to set in and then apply for total clearance aid. The proposed change 'may encourage municipalities to adopt and enforce by-laws governing the maintenance and occupancy of their housing stock and thus prevent rapid spread of blight.
It is now proposed, Mr. Chairman, to amend section 36 to permit the federal government to pay 75 per cent of the cost of

acquiring and rehabilitating existing housing, but this only in urban renewal areas designated by agreement among participating governments. In other words, it will be a corollary to the federal-provincial plans at the present time for subsidized housing. This amendment will enable a federal-provincial partnership to augment the stock of public housing with usable existing housing, at lower cost than is possible with new construction. We have a tremendous demand for such housing at the present time. We feel that this will aid the municipalities, and aid the federal government as well in providing more housing at lower cost. The federal government will continue to participate in worthy projects for new construction submitted by provinces on behalf of municipalities.
Hon. members will recall that the act contains provision for federal guarantees of bank loans for the improvement of existing housing. Before October of this year these guarantees were restricted to loans for the improvement of houses occupied by the owner. On October 11 I announced an extension of this N.H.A. assistance to an entirely new field of residential improvement and repair work. Home improvement loan financing under this act was extended to owners of rental properties, including apartment buildings, for structural alterations, interior and exterior decorating, plumbing, heating, electrical work and other improvements that qualify under the regulations. With our rental housing stock numbering 1,500,000 units, and with owners now eligible for National Housing Act bank loans, an extensive program of repair and improvement of the existing rental housing stock is now possible.
Think of it, gentlemen. With 1,500,000 rental units and with the possibility now of obtaining loans for their improvement, think of the possibilities for employment that are provided all across the country. I am sure that hon. members will appreciate the improvement in the quality of rental housing that may result, and the employment opportunities that this extension of the home improvement program will create. Because of this change it is proposed that the aggregate amount of loans that can be guaranteed under the act be increased from $200 million to $500 million.
In addition to all these changes in the present act I should like now to present a proposal that will add quite new purposes to the legislation and entirely new purposes to the work of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I am coming now to something that has always been in the mind of the Prime Minister. He has constantly thought of
National Housing Act
this, but has not been able, until now, to do a great deal about it. The first of these features is the provision of aid to those municipal works designed to reduce or eliminate the pollution of Canada's waterways. We heard a magnificent speech in this house a year or so ago from the hon. member for Carleton on the subject of pollution, and no words of mine could add to his exposition of the tremendous problem this represents today and will represent in the future unless immediate steps are taken to correct it. As a matter of fact, since the speech from the throne was publicized I have been besieged with calls from mayors of municipalities all over Canada to obtain particulars of the government's proposal. Of course, I have not been able to give them particulars until the bill was introduced in the house.
Great numbers of Canadians are now living in surroundings that are urban in every other respect except that they lack adequate sewage facilities. Less than one sixth of our urban municipalities have adequate sewage treatment plants in operation; perhaps two-thirds of our urban population are living in regions where seriously polluted surface waters are found. Quite a number of years ago I recall being retained by the riparian owners below a city. I was retained simply for the purpose of suing the town, and the town was delighted to be sued because that enabled it to get the provincial authorities to come forward with a grant which would permit the town to instal a sewage disposal plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman.
Under the housing act there has always been pressure to build houses in areas not yet provided with municipal sewerage service. This of course requires the house buyer to pay for a septic tank as part of his property. Several disadvantages then ensue because he will require a larger lot and hence more outlay for land and connections to all other services. Even with that safeguard great concentrations of these devices have made for soil pollution in many parts of the country. When trunk sewers and a treatment plant are finally installed the householder will find

National Housing Act
himself paying for duplicate sanitary devices, the earlier on his own property through his purchase price and the later on city property through his taxes. That situation presents a great problem to a great many people.
In order to avoid these difficulties we have tried to confine N.H.A. financing to houses connected to sewers. This effort has had other undesirable results. The amount of land within reach of a municipal sewage system has always been less than the amount of land required for such active house building programs as we have had in recent years, and so available sewered land has enjoyed scarcity values.
Residential areas are less well served with sewers than are other kinds of districts in our cities; newer residential areas are still more deprived, and land just about to be taken up for new housing is the worst off of all for sewers. Thus it has been decided to approach this problem directly by providing loans for municipalities to expand their sewerage systems, these loans to be made under a new part of the National Housing Act.
It is recognized that some provinces and municipalities are already launched on aggressive programs to redress defects in this part of their urban equipment. Indeed, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has quite specifically represented to us, not once but many times, that additional credit resources for this purpose would enable their member municipalities to move ahead much faster than they have been able to do up to the present time. As a matter of fact, the last such statement from them was made to our cabinet as recently as November 8.
Hence, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, we are bringing down a measure that will extend aid for purposes that everyone agrees must be served if Canadian urban development is to continue in vigorous, healthy and orderly fashion; and we are bringing it into the house in a form that focuses on the areas of most acute need and corresponds with the stated desires of Canadian local governments. Every local authority sincerely wishing to correct the evil of pollution will find through this measure a helping federal hand.

I am sorry to interrupt the minister but I should like to be clear on that point. By what he has just explained, does the minister mean that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the government will be ready to make loans or give subsidies for the construction of main sewers or trunk sewers or whatever he has called them?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am glad my friend the hon. member for Levis asked that question. They will be confined1 to sewage disposal plants and the trunk sewers and not the whole works. They will be confined to sewage disposal plants mainly and the trunk sewers.

I have just one other question for the purpose of explanation. Suppose there is a development in a new area in a city or that the city needs to replace its main sewer by a bigger one. Would that be covered by the new amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Provided that a sewage disposal plant is being installed. The details of all this matter can be worked out under the regulations. I will be giving the particulars when the bill is presented to the house. Does that satisfy the hon. member?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Because individual house connections are already financed in many cases by normal mortgage arrangements, this measure is confined to works of central plants and trunk main characteristics. It is intended that proposed work should be approved by competent provincial health authorities, and that the proposal to borrow under the National Housing Act should have provincial approval before C.M.H.C. will entertain a formal application for a loan. I should think, from past experience of cordial relations between municipalities and C.M.H.C. field offices, that informal consultation will usually precede the formal application. However, it is to be understood that the province will not be the middleman here. We shall be dealing directly with the municipalities; that is to say, the federal people will be dealing directly with the municipalities. Whatever the provinces want to do besides this is up to the provinces. We shall be glad to have them make whatever contributions they can make.
The amount of the loan is to be limited to two thirds of the cost of the proposed work as recognized by C.M.H.C. Just as in housing, C.M.H.C. will be the final arbiter. This loan will be repayable by the municipality over a long term of not more than 50 years, at a rate of interest close to the federal borrowing rate, just as the limited dividend rate is close to the government borrowing rate. Provision is made for loans to be made to a group of adjoining municipalities, a matter of some importance in our growing metropolitan areas where municipal boundaries do not always correspond with the limits of drainage basins. You will be asked to set aside $100 million for this purpose.
You will find that these loans are being made in order to step up this program and to inculcate in the municipalities the desire

for immediate action and also as an encouragement to take up some of the unemployed and put them to work. This whole program is designed to do that. To encourage the most vigorous attack on this problem the measure provides for one quarter of the C.M.H.C. loan to be forgiven where it is spent on work put in place by April 1, 1963. That provision should get the matter rolling right away. Many people have been inquiring, even today, as to when they could get started.
It is anticipated that advances will be made by C.M.H.C. to borrowing municipalities as their projects proceed and as evidence of the costs incurred is tendered to the corporation. A municipality will thus be able to take fullest advantage of the measure by programming its work so that completion is scheduled in the next two seasons.
Hon. members will appreciate that some administrative details remain to be settled by consultation between C.M.H.C. officers and officials of the provinces and municipalities. But what I have said should convince the committee of the government's determination that great strides to overcome this urgent need for major urban sewerage works will be taken all across Canada in the immediate future.
I now want to discuss another realm of legislation also to come under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and a matter in which I have been interested ever since I was in university. The second new feature proposed for the housing act is a provision to make loans to universities for students' residences. This, too, reflects a growing national need. The population sector of university age has been steadily increasing; increasing, as a matter of fact, by leaps and bounds. The actual enrolment of full-time students has risen from 63,500 in 1952 to about 100,000 today and is expected to reach the staggering total of 160,000 by 1966. In recognition of the national importance of our universities, the per capita base of federal grants to universities was increased in 1957 to $1.50.
The national conference of Canadian universities has reported that in 1958, 60 per cent of university students were domiciled 15 miles or more from their university. University residences could then accommodate only about one quarter of their out of town students. That was in 1958-it is much worse at the present time. Our universities are agreed that the advantages of life in student residences are no small part of the educational process. For this reason universities want a substantial increase in the capacity of their student residences. Such residences are needed if our universities are to fulfil their national function. Everyone here appreciates that university life is more complete
National Housing Act
and can afford greater advantages to the student if he has the opportunity of living in a university residence.
A number of university officials have in the past inquired whether the limited dividend section of the act, which offers advantageous lending terms, could be used to finance residential accommodation for students. However, I have had to tell them all that the present section emphasizes family housing in self-contained dwelling units and does not lend itself to this proposal. I think that at some time or other in the past year I have interviewed the presidents of at least eight universities, as well as other officials from other universities, all asking if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could do something to alleviate this very pressing problem.
Grants have been made by the Canada Council-which is, by the way, doing an excellent job-for the construction of a few student residences; but of course this source of assistance is limited. Furthermore, it requires an equal outlay of capital by the universities. Consequently, following representations made to us by the Canadian Universities Foundation, we propose to amend the National Housing Act to allow the corporation to make higher ratio loans at low interest rates for the construction of student residences at universities. The proposed loans may be up to 90 per cent of the cost of a project and are to bear the same rate of interest as limited divided loans. In other words, it is something like a limited dividend proposition. They may be made for a term not exceeding the useful life of the project, but in no case for more than 50 years.
Just a week ago the Prime Minister called me in to a conference with university presidents, and they were asked, if a program like this was undertaken by the government, how soon could the universities get under way to alleviate the unemployment problem. You will be very happy to learn that several of them stated that they had plans ready; all they needed in the past was financing, and they could get under way almost immediately, as soon as this proposed act was put into effect.
The growth of Canada's economic capacity has given the government the opportunity to deal with national needs that had to be deferred in earlier years. In a non-partisan vein, may I invoke the goodwill of the hon. members of this house to let us think big at the present time. We are proposing a program of tremendous scope and tremendous prospective results. The amendments to the National Housing Act which I have outlined reflect our sincere conviction that, among these

National Housing Act
unmet needs, improvement of the living conditions of the Canadian people must rank very, very high. With the resources of skill and materials available to us we can induce a large group of new home owners and entrepreneurs to enter the market. And every time you get a man and his family in a new home you have a Canadian who has a stake in the country; and the more people that we have owning homes, the better it will be for Canada. There is no question about that; that is a truism.
We can at the same time broaden the credit facilities for upkeep, repair and improvement of houses already occupied, in other words, rehabilitating existing housing. We can widen the scope of the combined operations necessary to the renewal and revitalization of our cities. We must recognize that the rapid expansion of these cities cannot go on without prompt attention to the grave conditions of pollution developing in some of our endowment of waterways. Much has been done under the housing act to provide dwellings for old people. We believe the next particular group of Canadians in urgent need are those young people leaving home to attend our universities, and on whose leadership the future of this nation may very well depend. Of all the measures that have been brought before this house, those which I have described should, I submit, have the highest priority.
All of the measures I have described will have a substantial and beneficial effect on employment. Just consider this. I cannot make any estimate for the hon. member for Nipis-sing of the number of people who will get employment, but the scope of this measure is tremendous for increasing employment. The greater opportunity for Canadian families to achieve home ownership will increase demand for housing and thus create employment opportunities resulting from an expanded housing program. At this time every house that is built gives six months' employment to two men on the job and two men off the job, and also another man who is employed getting the sewers, and so on, ready.
The extension of home improvement loans to rental housing will increase activity in the whole field of renovation and repair. And what a big field it is-1,500,000 houses. Canadian universities are anxious to proceed with expansion programs for student residences at once. The aids to municipalities for the
25 per cent for that work completed by the end of March, 1963 will, we are satisfied, be a very real inducement.
The fundamental purpose of this legislation is thus to improve housing conditions. Fundamentally, that is what it is. Also-and this is very important at this time the fundamental purpose of this legislation is to create jobs in ever growing numbers.
May I very respectfully add to what the Prime Minister said yesterday, that with the federal government, the ten provincial governments, the 5,000 municipal governments, contributed 15 per cent of the gross national product. It does not matter how we strive here at Ottawa, under the lashings of the Leader of the Opposition; it does not matter how we strive, how you strive, how the government of Canada, the provinces and all the municipalities strive, we are limited to 15 per cent of the gross national product.
The problem of employment is essentially a problem for all Canadians. We have a free enterprise system, and if we want to continue our free enterprise system, which produces 85 per cent of the gross national product of Canada, every Canadian-not just those engaged in the government of the country-must perform his or her very real and important task.

Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to thank the minister for the very comprehensive statement which he has just given the house on this very important subject. I would suggest that my only criticism is that this speech, and this action which is outlined now, should have been made much earlier, in fact, years ago.
May I say at once that the official opposition is most anxious to expedite the passage of this resolution and by so doing to assist in bringing in the legislation at the earliest opportunity. With this in mind, my remarks will be very brief. Naturally, too we are anxious to see the actual legislation envisaged by the resolution before we attempt to make any detailed analysis of it. Suffice it to say at this time that while the changes proposed seem to be changes in the right direction and so they should be, because they have been suggested in one way or another by the opposition-I do not feel they are adequate in themselves nor do I think they come to grips with the real problem at this time.
We are anxious to see the proposed legislation with respect to urban redevelopment because we have long been attempting to stress the urgent need in this field. Few countries are urbanizing as rapidly as Canada, and
rovision of sewerage trunks and plants will nable them to accelerate the pace of such zorks and thereby increase employment both n the site and in the plants manufacturing laterial and equipment; and this rebate of

there is an urgent need to speed up the redevelopment of the blighted areas in our cities. In recognition of this problem the

National Housing Act
Liberal party's resolutions as far back as 1958 suggested the setting up of a municipal grants assistance act under which the federal government would assist municipalities to in-stal essential services. We also proposed that there should be an increase from 50 per cent to 75 per cent in the federal share of joint slum clearance schemes.
During the last session of parliament Liberal suggestions to extend the scope of the winter works program would, if accepted, have provided further assistance to municipalities in redeveloping their cities and would have provided much needed work at the present time.
I should like to refer briefly to the reference in the resolution authorizing the corporation to make loans to assist the construction of sewage disposal projects. We are told now that this is in respect of sewage disposal projects. I suggest that this is a fine proposal, but I think it is much too limited, certainly as compared with the suggestion we made back in 1958 for a municipal loan fund.
This resolution seems to reflect a belated recognition of the government's own failure in the earlier part of the year to assess the housing and economic situation accurately. Never has there been a better example of wrong action and wrong timing than the government's housing policy, or patchwork policy, in 1960. Early in the year the government stubbornly stuck to a policy of retarding house building by slicing in half the money to be made available for direct lending. Later in the year, with evidence mounting every month that the housing program was a flop, the government attempted in July to inject a small dose of serum which failed to bring the patient out of the deep sleep deliberately encouraged by the government.
Now, near the end of 1960, with housing starts down by 30 per cent, with the result that many of our people are needlessly unemployed, the government seems ready to try some of the things it should have done earlier. However, I am afraid that in this respect hon. gentlemen opposite are locking the stable after the horse has been stolen. They seem ready now to try almost anything in order to get the house building industry back into business. The events of the past three years seem to me to indicate clearly that this government treats housing primarily as an economic pump primer, rather than realizing that good housing is as necessary to life as food, clothing and other necessities.
Proof that this government failed miserably to accurately assess the economic situation in 1960 is apparent in many fields. However, in the housing field they really goofed. No better example can be found than in the 90205-6-7J
New Year's message of the former minister of trade and commerce in which he stated there would be 140,000 housing starts in 1960. If anyone is interested I would be glad to enlarge on what he said at that time. Next, we had the Minister of Public Works announcing a policy of retarding house building and, at the same time, announcing the government's objective of 125,000 starts, down substantially as compared with the previous year's figures and supposedly necessary, according to the minister, in order not to overtax the boom which was hoped for in other segments of the construction industry.
We on this side pointed out that it would be impossible to build 125,000 homes under the policy existing at that time. The government kept insisting it could. Even with the housing program "beefed up" by several changes in mid-summer and during the fall, housing starts at the end of October stood at approximately 61,000 in areas of over
5,000	population, and I believe the total for the first nine months is approximately 76,000 for all areas.
Statistics published each month have proved how wrong the government was in its forecasts and appraisal of the situation. It is apparent they have been out of touch with the facts or, worse still, if they had the facts, that they have mishandled this important section of the economy.
I should like to make two observations which I feel are quite obvious. First of all, many of the changes made by the government during the last half of the year should have been made earlier if it was the intention to help the unemployment situation this winter. Second, we have now passed through a period of great scarcity of mortgage funds to a period where there is, rather, a great scarcity of purchasers of homes. Proof of this contention can be found in the Canadian housing statistics for October, which the minister yesterday refused to put on the record of this house. These figures show, first, that the approved lenders are pouring money into housing at these very attractive government-set N.H.A. rates. In fact, in the month of October, 1960 they placed 3,195 loans representing an increase in lending of 883 per cent as compared to a year earlier.
Proof that we have entered a period of increased buyers' resistance can be found in these October figures, too, which show a growing number of completed unoccupied homes-4,037, to be exact, or an increase of 28 per cent. This reluctance to buy and the build-up of completed unoccupied homes is especially significant when one realizes that housing starts are down 30 per cent in the first ten months of this year.

National Housing Act
The government should act now to meet this new situation, restore confidence throughout the economy, and work toward lowering the cost of housing. In my opinion the government has overlooked the real villain in the slowing down of housing. I believe the government should act at once and lower the maximum interest rate allowed under N.H.A. This government is responsible for artificially stimulating mortgage rates in this country with its ill-conceived conversion loan and huge deficits; deficits, I might add, that have failed to put our people to work. It would seem we are to have more of the same this year.
This artificial stimulation of the money market has increased the cost of housing, and especially the cost of financing housing, to the point where many of our people are reluctant to take on these heavy financing obligations. Now, under this administration, it costs more to finance a home than the purchase price. Therefore it is little wonder that buyers are hard to find. I believe the government should lead the way toward lower interest rates in this country. They will never have a better opportunity to lower the rate of N.H.A. borrowing from its present unprecedented high level of 6f per cent. Only by lowering the interest rate, and by so doing encouraging other lenders to follow suit, will we be able to bring the cost of housing down within reach of the average Canadian family to a degree that will adequately stimulate the industry, put many of our unemployed back to work, and make it possible for our people to have better housing, especially those in the medium and lower income groups.
As I said at the beginning we are looking forward to the early introduction of this legislation. At that stage we in the opposition will deal with the proposed changes in some detail and will I hope be able to offer to the government some further suggestions for improving this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this group I wish to express our welcome of the intentions the government has announced in this resolution. I am afraid I shall have to differ a little from the hon. member for Nipissing in a number of matters and especially in attitude.
In our opinion housing legislation is among the most important legislation. Our whole society depends to a great extent on the kind and number of homes in which the Canadian people live. We feel this is a field where political considerations should be disregarded and left out of the arguments. Housing is extremely important in respect

to the volume of employment. It is an important topic because we have a need for additional housing for our people today identical to the need for housing we had at the end of the war. Despite our efforts we have been able to do nothing more than keep pace with the needs of our increasing population and have not been able to abolish the backlog of housing needs that existed back in 1945. An active housing industry is important to all branches of Canadian industrial enterprise.
I am going to congratulate the government at this time because I feel that in the matter of housing the government has done more than it has in regard to any other department.
I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for the excellence of his detailed report. However, I wish to appeal to the minister and the government to recognize that even though in the past number of years great efforts have been made in the matter of supplying adequate housing there is much that yet remains to be done. I believe the minister would agree with that statement. Our problem is, in fact, growing in this respect because both rents and the prices of homes in Canada continue their upward climb. Until there is a decline in these levels it is obvious that we will have an insufficient number of adequate housing units, otherwise normal competition would be responsible for a reduction in rents and the retail prices of homes.
Other problems in connection with housing continue to grow. The number of available homes is inadequate and I cannot accept the argument of the minister that within recent times there has been a real weakness of demand. There may have been what economists would call an effective weakness of demand but I do not think the minister would want to claim that there were more houses available than there were Canadians really needing houses. The weakness of demand was the result of the inability of the people to purchase the housing offered. I think that ought to be recognized. I agree with the hon. member for Nipissing that the government made a mistake when it became unduly alarmed at an apparent weakness of demand a number of months ago and deliberately retarded expansion of the Canadian housing industry.
We have not today resolved the problem of those people who need housing most. We have not made it possible for them to obtain adequate housing at prices they are able to afford. The income class that has been helped by using the taxpayer's dollar is not the income class for whom the National Housing Act was really designed. When we use the

taxpayer's money for projects such as the supply of housing we have a moral obligation to Canadians to ensure that this money is used to supply assistance where it is most urgently needed. I realize the problems involved but all our efforts should be turned in this direction.
I endorse lowering of the interest rates. With the slowdown in industrial expansion on the Canadian economic scene there should be more investment capital available for housing than there was a year or so ago. Interest rates have declined. The over-all decline in interest rates and in the earnings of Canadian corporations ought to be reflected in the passing on of benefits to those who need housing by a lowering of the maximum interest rates that are permitted in this field.
We have noticed over a number of years that with a more massive amount of taxpayer's capital being invested by the government in housing, the less the private investors invest in housing. Perhaps the time has come when the government should take remedial action to prevent those who could invest money in housing deliberately deserting the housing field and re-entering it only when general profits and returns in industrial expansion are down. Willy-nilly they enter the field and withdraw at their own convenience and the government of the day is left holding the bag and has to take up the slack.
The government should have more jurisdiction over the flow of available investment capital within the nation so there could be a constant supply of investment money devoted to the needs of housing. We wish to see the establishment of a national investment board but changes would also be required in other legislation relating to the activities of Canadian insurance companies and other investment houses. The government ought to exercise more authority over the level of earnings that money can obtain elsewhere and over the maximum interest rates that can be charged throughout the economy. If the government exercised this authority there would be less difficulty persuading private capital to meet its responsibility in the field of housing.
I believe the resolution before us lacks any expression of intention on the part of the government to meet the need for additional low rental housing being made available to the Canadian people. There are millions of Canadians who do not desire home ownership. There are many millions of Canadians for whom home ownership is not realistic at all because of their income or because of the nature of their work, and there is an urgent need, when we use the taxpayer's money, to pay much more attention to the
National Housing Act
obtaining of many more units of low rental housing than has recently been the case.
When the government speaks of helping the municipalities I believe it might also extend the help it is giving or planning to give to the municipalities to make it possible to reduce the price of lots, and to do this by making money available to the municipalities so that they may be able to develop blocks of land to the point where they would be able to put the lots on the market and eliminate the operator who is responsible for the fantastic increase that we have witnessed in recent years in the price of lots, especially those in suburban areas.
I should like to bring another problem to the attention of the minister. I believe that perhaps one of the recommendations contained in the resolution will help in this regard. It is now relatively easy to build a house and obtain a mortgage in the high class areas of our larger metropolitan centres. It is also very easy to obtain a direct loan through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build a house in a little village many miles away from a metropolitan area. However, it is becoming almost impossible to obtain adequate financing to build houses in the areas around the metropolitan area or in the suburban area. At the present time, because of the way our policies are working out, we feel there is discrimination against suburban areas. While we used to complain of the urban sprawl, what is happening now is that those housing developments are taking place beyond the suburban areas, and a bad situation is becoming worse. Instead of going 15 miles into town to work, people now go 40 miles and 50 miles, because at distances 40 miles to 50 miles away they are able to buy a lot for very little money, and it is comparatively easy to get a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loan at that distance away from the city.
This is a problem that has to be met. Perhaps the government's plan to help municipalities to build disposal plants so that the lots in suburbia can be serviced may be a part of the answer. I am afraid that even more action may be necessary to call a halt to this leapfrogging over the suburbs and building large communities many miles away from where people work. I hope the plans of the government to assist in the building of such disposal plants are not designed only to prevent the pollution of rivers, because if they are this will discriminate against municipalities that will not be able to take advantage of the assistance offered since the disposal of the sewage of a great many municipalities has very little connection with the pollution of rivers. I hope it is the intention

National Housing Act
of the government to make this assistance available to all municipalities regardless of whether the disposal plant is designed primarily to prevent river pollution.
We also hope that when federal government money is involved it will insist that not less than union wages and working conditions ought to prevail. This has been the old rule, long since established, when government projects are undertaken. I should like to see this principle established and extended to the building of houses, if the taxpayer's money is used to supply the necessary capital.
The minister made a welcome announcement when he indicated that the lending ratio was to be raised from 90 per cent to 95 per cent and also the number of years for repayment were to be increased from 30 to 35. I hope the minister realizes that when he raises the lending ratio he increases the monthly payment. He is attempting to offset this by adding to the number of years. I should like to pose the problem to him which this represents to a person over 30 years of age. In most plants in Canada the normal retirement age is 65. I am afraid that a large number of people who have been eligible under the old arrangement, and who are past the age of 30, will now become ineligible because, as the minister knows, very many people are just on the borderline of being eligible. Any increase in the amount of monthly payments immediately results in the disqualification of many applicants and this would apply in many cases. I know the minister's extension of the years remedies it, but it remedies it only for the younger people. It is not a remedy for the man who is past the age of 30.
I had hoped that the minister might have made some announcement indicating that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could in some way be a greater help in the building of a beautiful national capital. I am very disappointed at the slow progress we are making in the beautification of our nation's capital. I was lucky over the week end a while ago to be in Washington, and it made me horribly ashamed of conditions in our own capital. I feel that those conditions are becoming worse as time goes by, and especially as we observe what other countries are doing. I think this legislation might be amended in such a way that much more effective aid might be given to the people of Ottawa to beautify their city.
The minister mentioned that aid was to be given for part of the cost of the surveys to provide for urban renewal in order to eliminate blighted areas in our cities. I should like to plead with the minister and urge that the federal government ought also to

assume responsibility for paying for a part of the cost when a municipality, or a group of municipalities, want to conduct housing surveys for the purpose of preventing the development of blighted or slum areas. I believe municipalities ought to be encouraged to prevent slums, as they ought also to be encouraged in the matter of the removal of slums.
The help to the universities is most welcome indeed. I had hoped that the government would have found the necessary money to make at least a partial grant toward the construction of those residences. In this connection I should like to call the minister's attention to an old request of ours. He knows very well that when we build cottages and apartment blocks for the benefit of our retired senior citizens and others on low income our provincial government in British Columbia makes a contribution of one third of the capital cost. Ottawa helps, but only by lending us roughly two thirds, or a little less than two thirds of the capital cost, which has to be repaid with interest even though it is interest at a reduced rate. I feel that if our provincial governments are able to make a contribution of one third of the cost of housing for our senior citizens on low incomes, our national government should not do less.
I believe, in connection with residences for our universities, which admittedly are most urgent, that a contribution or cancellation of a part of the loan by the federal government might receive some consideration.
I began by saying that in our opinion much has been done by this government in the field of housing. However, we believe that this government ought to realize that, in the field of housing at least, free enterprise has completely failed. The minister spoke of the need to maintain free enterprise, but I think he must admit that in this field it has completely failed the needs of the Canadian people. There is much more that remains to be done. In the interests of the housing needs of our people, in the interests of employment, in the interests of giving a shot in the arm to our whole economy, we believe that the government should add much more to what I will admit are the many proposals it has now placed before the house.

National Housing Act
year on their capital budget which would enable them to look after this urban redevelopment in a very orderly way.
For example, in Hamilton they broke down the acreage in this blighted area and found that the cost would be over $106,000 per acre. Unless very serious consideration is given to this problem and encouragement given to private enterprise to go into this business of slum clearance and redevelopment, I think it will be a long time before we clear up the problem in Hamilton. I am confident that with a man of the calibre of Mr. Ken Soble, a very prominent Hamilton businessman who is chairman of this committee, and the vigorous management of Paul Goyette of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we will go a long way toward solving this problem.
I do not want to delay the passage of this resolution, but I do want to congratulate the minister at this time for giving us the first complete look at mortgage and housing policy in this country through such things as land development, sewage disposal and lower down payments on houses. The program even includes the universities. I feel this is the best program for development, taking a long range view rather than plugging the holes in the dike every time they appear. I feel we will do a service to Canada on a long range basis, and I think we will all benefit very much from it.

First, I should like to congratulate the minister. He certainly has done a fine job in introducing this legislation. I fought for it last summer. We wanted it, and now we have it. I believe the minister has done a real job. The part of Canada from which I come is very large, almost as large as Texas or larger. One gentleman says they are playing leapfrog to get lots. I may tell you that for 300 miles or 400 miles from where I am all the lots are sold there. I do not know what they are going to build there. Maybe they are waiting for housing projects to come along. We are a people of young families. Our birth rate is high. The children of today are the citizens of tomorrow. That is why I like to see housing projects come along. People cannot sleep in tents; they must be housed. The country from which I come is a cold one. It is not like California or anything like that. I believe we should give all young couples a chance to get homes of their own and produce good citizens.
I am just going to say once more that I congratulate the minister. I am thankful for what he has done. It certainly helps my country. In Dawson Creek no carpenters are out of work. I talked to one contractor. He said, "I have enough work this winter in these houses that are being built to keep

my men all employed". I suppose that in Prince George the situation is the same. The man who is out of work is the shovel man, the manual labourer. A man told me the other day that he went over to the Bell Telephone Company in order to try to get a job in that company. He was asked whether he had a grade 12 education. He said that is the first time he had ever heard of anybody requiring to have a grade 12 education in order to use a pick. 1 just want to say that I am pleased with the legislation coming in and I will let some of the rest of the sharp-shooters tell you all about it.

I too of course want to congratulate the government on this forward step. But before the minister brings in his bill I want to make a special plea for a special kind of community. I refer to the centre of population which has 6,000 people,
7,000	people or fewer. I can speak particularly well of the district I represent which is at the moment bursting at the seams, and I mean that literally.
At the northern end of my constituency we have the town of Leduc which touches on the new Edmonton international airport. It is going to require a major housing development. As the minister knows, I have been in his hair somewhat all summer trying to get money for this purpose. I am hoping that special provision will be made for places like that.
In the city of Wetaskiwin we have the hope and the very good prospect of a plant being built by the Carnation Milk Company early in 1961. In this city there are 5,600 people. We will require housing money.
In another part of my constituency, in between the towns of Ponoka and Rimbey, we have nearing completion the largest gas extraction plant on the North American continent. This plant will bring a major influx of workers to my constituency. They will need housing. These are two towns of 4,000 and 2,000 respectively. In Lacombe we hope to have a new meat packing plant built.
As can be seen, these are centres in which there is far greater need than there is in the large metropolitan areas. Unlike my friend from the west coast who spoke about leapfrogging, we do not have that situation. I think everybody will agree that today the trend is not toward more living in the large centres but to an effort to raise families in the smaller centres where there is room for children to grow. The children of today are the citizens of tomorrow. I think we should give them this opportunity for a better life which this legislation will give. I think we should think of these smaller centres which up

until now have had a great deal of difficulty in getting house building money. I would hope the minister would give that matter serious consideration in this new bill.

I should like to add these few words of congratulation to the Minister of Public Works for having introduced this resolution. He has introduced one of those types of programs which I have advocated for a long time and I believe it will have far-reaching effects in the country. I rise to speak on it because I wish to bring out a few points which have not been mentioned by those who have spoken previously.
I want to say concerning the resolution that the housing provision should be very far-reaching, particularly in the urban areas. University housing is greatly needed and it will serve an extremely useful purpose supplementing the work which has already been started by the Canada Council.
The loans and rebates to municipalities for the construction of sewage projects for the elimination of pollution is one of the items which was discussed in the committee on mines, forests and waters last year. We recommended that action be taken on this particular project and that everything should be done to eliminate the waste and sewage which is pouring from most of our cities throughout the land into streams which flow thereby. For example, speaking of the city of Ottawa and the Ottawa river, I am told that the sewage from this city is dumped directly into the river or thereabouts and that there is the equivalent of about 50 dead horses going by a given point in that river every hour. Surely we, as a civilized people, as people who make the claim that we are ahead of others in other lands, should put forth every effort to correct this situation. This part of the resolution should go a long way toward assisting in that respect.
There is in this resolution another aspect that has not been brought out on which I should like to touch. The resolution deals primarily with urban areas. I happen to represent a rural area in southwestern Alberta. I should like to see better water brought into some of the drier communities and towns that are now in great need of a better quality of water. For instance, in some of these rural community centres the people are unable to obtain water except from wells; and often the wells contain water which is so polluted with alkali that they are unable to drink it without a tremendous amount of softening and even then it is unsuitable for putting on gardens and for other uses. What is needed, and what some of these centres are contefn-plating doing, is to tap reservoirs of good 90205-6-8
National Housing Act
water at distances of from 10 miles to 15 miles to 20 miles and pipe in the good soft water. But they are hesitating to do this because they need loans. They need assistance in order to put in these water systems.
I do not wish to minimize the necessity of having pollution taken care of in the urban centres but I urge the government to give full consideration to the rural areas and above all to give priority to bringing good water to these rural centres which are so much in need of good water. In other words balancing the need within the country when it comes to government assistance and loanable funds. It seems to me that the need for good water ranks equally with solving the problem of sewage pollution. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I hope the government will take into consideration this problem of having good water piped into rural areas.
Before closing I should also like to again compliment the Minister of Public Works for what he has done and to say that I take great pleasure in supporting this resolution which he has brought before the house.

Mr. Chairman, like all previous speakers it gives me great pleasure to congratulate the government, and particularly our active minister, for this most welcomed piece of legislation. All people in Canada have an interest in most aspects of this resolution. I can recall a few years ago serving on a municipal council, and the plight of the municipality was great; it was nearly impossible to keep up with the growth and to maintain main trunk lines in order to have serviced lots for the extension of the new housing starts.
A great many of our hon. members have been to university, and all of us who have had the privilege of attending university recognize that one misses a great deal if one cannot participate in campus activities. It is unfortunate that the former secretary of state for external affairs, the Hon. Sidney Smith, is not with us tonight. On many occasions I discussed university problems with him. I know he would have welcomed this legislation, in so far as it will give aid to universities, as much, or more so than any of us present.
The housing aspect of it deserves our commendation. Since the C.M.H.C. legislation went on the statute books housing has had a great boost in Canada. During the years between 1950 and 1960 we have witnessed a great many new starts in this country. The legislation contemplated in this resolution will make it possible for thousands of our younger citizens to build new homes forthwith, immediately after their marriages. This

National Housing Act
will make it possible for them, as young married couples, to take a particularly active interest in community life.
Those who prefer to live in rental accommodation should receive an improvement in their living standards. The 1,500,000 rental units referred to by the minister are in some cases not too much credit to some of our municipalities.
However, it is the university aspect of the legislation in which I am most particularly interested. I hope the university presidents and those in charge of the universities-the boards of governors and trustees-will forthwith take advantage of this legislation. Ninety per cent of the amount can be borrowed, as stated by the minister, and it can be spread over a long period of years, up to fifty. This should make it possible for all universities of Canada to immediately-after plans have been prepared-take advantage of this program.
Most of the unemployment in the Atlantic provinces is in unskilled construction and the trades. Housing, of course, gives a great deal of winter work for tradesmen throughout the country. However, larger buildings such as university residences will make it possible for many of these projects to be continued throughout the winter months with little or no interruption because of snow.
The municipalities, through the union of mayors and municipalities, have been urging the government of Canada each and every year to make it possible for the municipalities to obtain money at a more reasonable rate of interest. The winter works programs have been expanded this year; it is now possible to build libraries, fire halls, et cetera. This government has made that possible. This new aspect of assistance introduced tonight should be of great benefit to all municipalities, and I believe it is to the credit of the union which fought so hard for the proposals.
Mr. Chairman, in my few remarks I want to once again thank the minister, and in conclusion, I would ask the people of Canada who intend to build new homes to do so at the first opportunity. I encourage the municipalities to take advantage of the new lending rules in order that they may be able to get their refunds. This must be done by them before 1963. I know that the universities and the alumni concerned will appreciate the aid which it is intended to give to them.
Jobs for construction workers and tradesmen appear on the upgrade; and not only those who are associated with the construction industry but the suppliers of building materials will welcome this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, it gives me pleasure to rise after the members who spoke before me, not to sum up the question, as I shall probably not be the last to discuss it, but to remind the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) of this French axiom which I know he will readily understand, being quite proficient in the French language: Quand le batiment va, tout va.
Mr. Chairman, I have seldom seen-

-so practical and so effective a piece of legislation as the one proposed in this resolution. It is one of the best ways of getting the government close to the people, from whom the former government had gotten away.
Mr. Chairman, my constituency is located close to Quebec city, and quite naturally, it receives the overflow of the city's expanding population. The constituency of Que-bec-Montmorency now has a population of about 125,000, distributed in 36 municipalities.
It follows that the measure now before us, which provides for improvements to existing houses and for urban redevelopment, will provide employment for many workers in that section of the country. For the young people wishing to settle down outside Quebec city, it will be easier to build a home where they can raise a family.
Mr. Chairman, since my election to parliament, I have had opportunities to hear the complaints of some municipal councils around Quebec city; now most of their problems revolved around the lack of funds for building sewers. Therefore, I feel sure that this wise piece of legislation put forth by the government will help the municipalities deal with this problem, which has become extremely serious. Moreover, Mr. Chairman, as I am representing a constituency in which Laval University is located, I cannot but congratulate the government for giving additional facilities for the building of students' residences. Indeed, the lack of housing, more particularly meant for students, was an almost insurmountable difficulty, and I am satisfied that a considerable proportion of the people in the neighbourhood of the city of Quebec as well as all students from the province of Quebec and of the whole country will be able to benefit from this legislation.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation pointed out that within the next 20 years, about 3,200,000 new houses would have to be built in this country, which means an

average of about 160,000 homes a year. Consequently, we find that, under the legislation now before this house, the government means to introduce some measure of regularity with regard to home building in this country and in this respect it deserves to be commended. All municipalities in this country, and more particularly those who are located close to larger cities, will benefit from the legislation and, as the representative of a constituency which I may call a suburban riding, I am happy to thank and to commend the government for having shown such wisdom and foresight in introducing this legislation.
