The reason I intervene in this debate is because of what was said by the hon. member for Westmorland about the importance of assisting universities in the construction of residences. I have had something to do with universities. For many years we were utterly wanting in residences at Queen's University. Lately we have been able to supply the need to some extent and I am glad to think we shall be able to go on, because I do believe that a great deal of benefit is acquired by students who are able, outside the classrooms and away from formal instruction, to exchange views with each other.
Another reason I intervene is to give a little illustration going back some years which will give the opinion on this subject of a man whose opinions I valued highly- a professor at Queen's University who was commanding a field company of engineers during the first world war. One summer evening, in 1916 or 1917 I strolled across and found him playing poker with his subalterns. He said: "Do you know, I could be court martialled for doing this?" Then he said, "Take a hand". I said, "I do not know how to play". "But you were at Queen's University" he replied. I had to explain I had lived at home. This was, he said, a great misfortune. "If my son goes to a university, if it is in the town where I am living I will send him out to live, even if it is in the house next door". I mention this for what it is worth, so that hon. members may know the value he attached to residences.
I wish to make one further point. We may well have reached the stage where public investment, investment in all kinds of things owned by the public and for the benefit of the public-roads, hospitals, universities and so on-may come to play a larger part in our economy than they have in the past. For 90205-6-81
National Housing Act
that reason, among others, I am very glad that the minister has brought down this measure.

I wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Public Works upon introducing this measure to amend the National Housing Act of 1954. There are some things in which I am particularly interested. One of them is the arrangement for loans to universities for the building of residences for students. I think that is a commendable proposal. Rooming houses now are totally inadequate to look after our students. Our university population has doubled, in a few years and in the very near future it will double again, so I think the government is on very sound ground when it makes these loans. I am also interested in the loans and rebates to the municipalities to assist in the building of sewage projects and for the elimination of pollution.
It is on this point particularly that I wish to speak but 1 would first of all like to make a few general comments if I may.
It is interesting to note that about one tenth of all the people in Canada now live in accommodation which has been provided for in the last five years, and that about 100,000 new homes have been built in the last four years for those with lower incomes. It has been said, and said with some truth, that housing is catching up, but I would remind the house, if indeed it does need reminding, that new births now number in Canada 400,000 per year and that very soon we shall need
200,000	new dwellings per year for young married couples establishing homes. In addition we shall also need homes for immigrants who may come to our shores, homes to take the place of those which have been cleared away under slum clearance projects and homes to replace those which have served their day and generation. We must not only permit more and more people to own their own homes, but we must see to it that they do. Every home owner has a deeper feeling of his responsibility to his community and country.
Now I return to the question of the rebates to the municipalities in respect to the building of sewage plants and for the elimination of pollution. As we have been told, two thirds of the cost is to be loaned to the municipalities over a period of years and if the work is completed by 1963, 25 per cent of this cost will be returned. It is certain that there are many towns and cities throughout Canada which could benefit from this legislation. Fewer than one sixth now have proper sewage facilities. Those municipalities with foresight and vision will be encouraged to deal with this problem and prepare themselves for the future.

National Housing Act
I know cases of towns which stand still simply because they lack sufficient water supplies and sewage disposal facilities. Factories establish themselves elsewhere where they can obtain properly serviced areas with water and sewage disposal facilities. I have in mind one small village which has a factory on the lake; the lake is polluted by the effluent from this factory, and it does not need much imagination to realize that in this great tourist area pollution of this kind simply must stop as soon as possible. I am wondering if this resolution will go far enough to enable the municipality to help build a sewage disposal plant for this factory to control the effluent and raw sewage which is going into the lake.
A similar situation exists in many lakes throughout the province. Cottagers decline to live near these polluted areas. Tourists refuse to stay there. People will not build motels or accommodation on such lakes to provide accommodation for the travelling public. These problems must be cleared up. The government should be commended for this farsighted policy because these problems must be cleared up in the municipalities if our water supply is to be kept free of pollution.
If the lakes to which I referred are cleaned up many tourists will come to the area. As a result of the government's action in making available loans to small business it will be possible to construct motels and hotels on the waterway to bring to the area the tourist dollars which are so urgently needed. In addition to that, the building of sewage disposal plants in the area will provide work for many people in the building trades and will enable the factory to operate in a satisfactory manner providing work for approximately 50 to 75 employees in this case I have in mind.
I am sure that a similar situation obtains in many Canadian municipalities. I am convinced that in many areas where there are septic tanks they are not doing the job due to poor drainage. Sewage disposal plants could be installed and that is up to the municipality at the ground level.
Not long ago I passed through a town where it was possible to smell the odour of the sewage overflow from the septic tank. The sewage was not being properly carried away by the tile drainage. Action in instances like this should be instituted at the municipal level. I am sure no effort at the present time the government could undertake would make a greater contribution to the sanitary facilities and welfare of individuals in Canada than the measure under which it would be possible for municipalities to receive assistance in the construction of sewage disposal projects.

I commend the minister for bringing this far-sighted proposal before the committee.
I am sure all hon. members opposite will welcome this measure that will assist in some measure in the installation of proper sanitary facilities throughout the length and breadth of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there is an aspect to this plan which greatly appeals to me at this time. It now appears that Canadian municipalities will be able to borrow money in Canada and this at a time when the present government has been accused of adopting a tight money policy. I believe for the first time in history Canadian municipalities will be able to obtain as much credit as they need for at least two major building projects by borrowing the money at home, regardless of interest rates. This will tend to balance off the Canadian economy and it is my earnest hope that the applicable interest rates will be exceedingly reasonable. It is a matter of great interest to me that Canadian municipalities will be able to borrow on the Canadian market. It has always been a mystery to me why they have not been able to borrow on the Canadian market previously. I am quite sure that the National Housing Act has not been used for this purpose. If this is to be one of the few sources of Canadian credit to our own municipalities, I am pleased to see this door opened. I hope the whole program will be greatly expanded along these lines.

I do not want to delay the progress of this resolution but I do want to add to what was said by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton South, concerning the remarks made by the hon. member for Nipissing. His comments on the remarks of the hon. member for Nipissing were made in anger whereas mine will be made more in sorrow than in anger.
Apparently the hon. member for Nipissing has not been listening to his party leader who since the last election has been roaring around the country promising programs and outlining patterns of government activity running into billions and billions of dollars. If the hon. gentleman had listened to the statements made by his leader and his leader's lieutenants the word "deficit" would have been the last word he would have used in this debate.

If the cap fits, wear it. In a general vein, the longer the present minister remains as Minister of Public Works the more he seems to contribute by his efforts to

reflect his observations in and around the area he represents, and certainly the field under his jurisdiction reflects a developing pattern of progress. That is all to the good.
I endorse the basic principle that he follows of studying the general situation, participating in this report of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada on the design of the residential environment-in other words the basic and logical approach of examining the problem in detail, holding hearings across the country and in this House of Commons- and then proceeding in logical phase to develop the pattern of measures which has been presented to the house.
It is interesting to note in passing that several of the recommendations of the R.A.I.C. have already been put into effect in part by this resolution. Again, following the basic logic in sequence, there is a general examination of the problem as it exists across all areas of the country, and then there is the introduction of positive definite measures to aid in the elimination of the blights in our major centres; the arrest of the deterioration by offering assistance along the lines the minister indicated; the stabilizing of those perimeter areas which cannot be classified as blights but given the normal progression would be so classified in a few years; and then the positive thrust forward in connection with the assistance and long term loans for sewage disposal plants which will affect the suburban areas.
I wish to assure the minister that these developments and the details that will be made known when we see the bill will be good news indeed to my constituency. I think that can also be said with respect to other constituencies in the Toronto area. One of the municipalities in my constituency, Scarborough, will be most interested in the sewage disposal proposition put forward by the government. Perhaps that municipality has already expressed its interest.
The aid to universities for student accommodation will be most welcome. A few weeks ago I had the good fortune to visit a number of maritime universities. In one instance alone which I vividly recall I was told by the faculty that over 1,000 students could not be accepted by that university for the simple reason that there was not accommodation available for those students in the campus area. In many university centres in Canada and particularly in the maritimes where the university is an important segment of the town there simply are not adequate facilities in the town for students wishing to attend university. The announcement of assistance will be most welcome not only to the university to which I referred but to universities across Canada.

Returning to my own constituency, there is a real possibility that York University will ultimately come within the vast boundaries of York-Scarborough and no doubt student residence assistance will be most effective in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I should very much like to associate myself with other hon. members who have congratulated the minister and the government and expressed their satisfaction with the legislation proposed in this resolution. This resolution is one of those items in the government's plans which is designed to bring about a greater measure of buoyancy in our economy at the present time for the purpose of creating and expanding job opportunities in this country, and it will be welcomed by all Canadians. Since I live in west Middlesex I represent an area which is composed partly of a suburban area, the city of London, several fair sized towns and villages and a large rural area. Nearly every item in this resolution is of great importance to our people of Middlesex West.
First of all I should like to deal with the matter of loans to municipalities for the purpose of promoting and encouraging the construction of sewage projects for the elimination of pollution in our streams and lakes. Down through that area where the country is densely populated the streams which once flowed with clear sparkling water are now little more than open sewers, and sewage disposal throughout the whole area of southwestern Ontario is one of the major problems facing the people there. The streams flowing through west Middlesex, the Thames below the city of London, the Sydenham below the town of Strathroy, the Ausable below several villages and towns along its course are polluted to the extent that they no longer serve as a source of pleasure for the residents of the area, and anything which can be done to remedy that pollution problem will be more than welcome to the people of our area.
I should like to associate myself particularly with those who have commended the government and the minister on including or offering to include a provision in this legislation for long term loans to municipalities for this purpose, and particularly the provision which would write off one quarter of the cost of those projects which are completed before 1963.
The provision also to increase the ratio for loans will be welcome news to the people in our area. It seems very difficult for people to buy and pay for houses today unless both parents are in a position where they can take a paying job. Of all the people who need houses and homes it is the people with

growing families. Where a smaller down payment is required it will make it much easier for families with limited incomes to own their own houses. I am sure that increasing the loan ratio will be of great assistance to people in the lower income brackets. Then, again, the extension of the period of repayment will help to cut down the size of the monthly payment and make houses more available to those with limited incomes.
The suggestion has been made that people of middle age who enter into a long term contract have little hope of completing the contract. I do not think that is any serious objection to long term contracts. When payments on houses can be reduced to the equivalent of rent, as they have been in the last few years and as they tend to become under the long term contracts, it does not greatly matter whether people complete the contract or not; they have a house at a rate which they are able to pay. After all, the provision of a house at a rate they are able to pay is the important thing.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

the National Housing Act, followed by second reading of the bill dealing with the guarantee on loans made by banks to proprietors of small business enterprises. On Thursday we shall continue with those measures, if they are not concluded on Wednesday. Under the rules, Thursday would normally be a private members' day. The rules call for the first two Thursdays after the conclusion of the speech from the throne being private members' days. The amendment to the rule made last session permits private members' Thursday to be deferred for one week. It is the intention on this occasion to do that, so government business will be conducted on Thursday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could the house leader give some indication what we might be doing on Monday?

speechtext: Again, the first six Mondays following the conclusion of the speech from the throne, according to the rules, are given over to private members' business unless superseded by a supply motion. It may be that that will be done on this occasion because, as it stands now, we would have Thursday of next week for private members' business, and I feel the house would not wish to take two days next week for private members matters. 1.	Were invitations to tender advertised for the bar and cocktail lounge privileges at the new air terminal building at Dorval?
2.	If so, what are the names of those who submitted tenders and the amount of their respective tenders?
3.	Was the contract awarded to the highest bidder?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport):
1.	No.
2 and 3. Answered by No. 1.
Note: It is not the practice of the department to call tenders for the operation of bar and cocktail lounge privileges in air terminal buildings. The department calls tenders for the operation of the restaurant concession in terminal buildings. Whether or not the successful tenderer for the restaurant concession in the terminal building subsequently is in a position to provide beverage service is a matter for the concessionaire to determine
in accordance with applicable provincial or municipal law, i.e. it is the responsibility of the concessionaire to obtain any licences or permits necessary in this connection.

1.	How many insurance companies presently underwrite the group surgical-medical insurance
plan?
2.	Are federal government employees entitled to use the facilities of the credit union and co-operative health services society of British Columbia? If not, for what reason?
Answer by: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
1.	Twenty six insurance companies presently underwrite the group surgical-medical insurance plan of which one is the principal underwriter and administers the plan, while the remaining 25 participate on a reinsurance basis.
2.	The credit union and co-operative health services society of British Columbia is not one of the companies mentioned above but, since participation in the group surgical-medical insurance plan is voluntary, federal government employees who wish to make private arrangements for their insurance with the credit union and co-operative health services society of British Columbia are free to do so.
